en: The Mahāvaipulya Amogha-sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty. Chapter One:
The Great Assembly’s Vigor; First Part of the Great Cloud: The First Section on the Great Assembly’s Vigor.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of ninety-eight thousand bhikṣus, headed by Mahākāśyapa and others. All of them were great arhats—whose outflows were exhausted and who had attained mastery; whose minds were as supple and well-tamed as those of the king of fragrant elephants;
who followed the path of goodness and had attained liberation of mind; and whose wisdom was unimpeded as they had laid down their heavy burdens.
Having accomplished what was to be done and forever severed all modes of existence (*bhava*), they had cultivated the prohibitive precepts and reached the further shore with a pure and subtle mind;

possessing towering majesty and great renown, they were fully endowed with and had attained the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). All of them, rising from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves before him with their heads to the ground, joined their palms in reverence, and circumambulated him three times to the right. Having completed these acts of veneration, they withdrew and sat to one side.

Furthermore, there was a community of sixty-five thousand bhikṣuṇīs, with the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī at their head. They also rose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit on one side.
Furthermore, there were sixty-eight thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were great fragrant elephant kings (*gandhahastirāja*).

Their names were: the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Great Cloud Secret Treasury (*Mahāmeghaguhya-garbha*), the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Great Cloud Attained-Vow (*Mahāmeghaprāptamanas*), the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Great Cloud Lightning-Light (*Mahāmeghavidyutprabha*), and the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Great Cloud Thunder-Resonance (*Mahāmeghagarjita*).
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-udyoga-garbha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-preman,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-pramoda, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-svabhāva,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-vajraśiras, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-ratnaśiras.
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmegha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmeghagarjita, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmeghakīrti,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmeghapraṇidhipuṣpa, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmeghavṛṣṭidāna,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmeghānādhyamāna, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmeghaprayukta.
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud Lion’s Roar King, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud Rain-Filling Mind King,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud Universal Radiance, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud Right View;
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Pervasive Rain King, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Body-Supernormal-Power King,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Supreme Excellence, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Sovereignty,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Great Ocean, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud All-Sovereignty.
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud Field of Merit, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud Bestower of All Peace and Security,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud Sunlight, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud Moonlight,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud Lapis Lazuli Light, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud [Unobstructed...]
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mātrika, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-nityadarśin,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-ātmadarśin, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-viśuddhadarśin,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-ratidarśin;
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Unhindered, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Ever-Victorious,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Pure Light, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Attaining Renown,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Cherishing Life, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Merchant Lord.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-Ānucara, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-Prakāśamārga,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-Guptaputra, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-Vijayapuṇḍarīka,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-Jvālāprabha, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmegha-Padma.
...the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva [named] *Mahāmegha*, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva *Mahāmeghopalagarbha*,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva *Mahāmeghatejorāja*, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva *Mahāmeghacalita*,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva *Mahāmeghaviśārada*, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva *Mahāmeghatamālapatrasītalā*...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Red Sandalwood Tree Coolness, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Utmost Depth,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Knowing the Good Teacher, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Nārāyaṇa Great Joy, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Great Bull King.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud King of Great Trees, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Dharma-White Lotus in Full Bloom,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Upholder of the Light of Dharma, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Renowned King-Gate,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Virtuous King of the Golden Mountain.
...the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Fearless King, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Great Physician King,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Great Body King, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Space King,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Cultivated Hair King, and the Great Cloud Destroyer of Clouds...

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of Wind that Shatters Great Clouds, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of Rain that Shatters Great Clouds, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of the Periphery of Great Clouds,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of Darkness-Cutting Great Clouds, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of Hail-Cutting Great Clouds.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmegha Kāśyapa and other such Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas likewise arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.
Furthermore, there were fifty-eight thousand Licchavi youths, whose names were: Lion-Light Licchavi, Dharma-Virtue Licchavi, Dharma-Longing Licchavi;
Śakra-Virtue Licchavi, Śakra-Banner Licchavi, Śakra-Pennant Licchavi, Lion’s Roar Licchavi, Jewel-Bell-Sound Licchavi, Love-Virtue Licchavi, Noble-Virtue Licchavi, and Vajra.
Śūli-cakra, Buddha-dāsa-li-cakra, Tathāgata-dāsa-li-cakra,
Bhagavat-dāsa-li-cakra, Bhagavān-dāsa-li-cakra, Samyaksaṃbuddha-dāsa-li-cakra, Bhagavat-candra-dāsa-li-cakra,
Mahāhasta-li-cakra, Mahāvīrya-li-cakra, Gaṅgāprāpta-li-cakra, and Mañjuśrī.
Śrīliṅga Licchavi, Maitreya Licchavi, Mahānāga Licchavi, Nāgarakṣita Licchavi,
Dharmarakṣita Licchavi, Viśvavikhyāta Licchavi, Gaganamegha Licchavi, Gaṅgārakṣita Licchavi,
Suvarṇapuṣpa Licchavi, Vidyutprabha Licchavi, Mahāviśālavadana Licchavi, and Svabhāvaviśāla.
Licchavi, Śuddhābha Licchavi, Vaiśravaṇa Licchavi, Mahābhūmika Licchavi,
Bhūmimāla Licchavi, Vaipulya Licchavi, and Vajra Licchavi.

All these Licchavis likewise had each resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they protected the Mahāyāna and delighted in the Mahāyāna, and all whom they taught were directed toward the Mahāyāna. They also arose from meditative concentration in the early morning and went to where the Buddha was. Prostrating with their heads at his feet, they joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed their acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.
Furthermore, there were forty-four thousand celestial kings (*deva-rāja*), whose names were: the Celestial King Priyadarśana (Love-View),
the Celestial King Sarvapriya (All-Love), the Celestial King Candrakeśa (Moon-Hair), the Celestial King Sūryavarṇa (Sun-Color), the Celestial King Dīrghakarṇa (Long-Ear),

the Celestial King Nīlavarṇa (Blue-Color), the Celestial King Vīrya (Diligence), the Celestial King Gambhīranetra (Deep-Eye), the Celestial King Mahākāla (Great Black), and the Celestial King Dūraprajña (Far-Wisdom).
The Deva King, the Deva King Ākāśanetra, the Deva King Priyaguṇa, the Deva King Priyakeśa,
the Deva King Priyanāmaprabha, the Deva King Priyamukhaprabha, the Deva King Sarvaprītimat, the Deva King Vaiḍūryaprabha,
the Deva King Prabhāpriya, the Deva King Ardhacandra, and the Deva King Mahāsvaramanojña.
The Celestial King Valiant Destroyer of Afflictions, the Celestial King All-Love, the Celestial King Child-Love,
the Celestial King Mandārava Flower, the Celestial King Impermanence, and the Celestial King Belonging to the Pleiades (Kṛttikā).
These great celestial kings—those who delight in the Mahāyāna, extensively expound the Mahāyāna, and protect and uphold the Mahāyāna;

who receive and maintain all samādhis and dhāraṇīs, and bestow upon sentient beings matters of peace and happiness—likewise arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.
Furthermore, there were thirty-eight thousand nāga kings, namely: the Nāga King Padma, the Nāga King Takṣaka,
the Nāga King Karkara, the Nāga King Vāsuki, the Nāga King Priyaguṇamālā,
the Nāga King Mahīdhara, the Nāga King Daṃṣṭrāla, the Nāga King Viśuddhanetra, and the Nāga King Siṃha.
Śaṅkhaśabda Nāgarāja, Bherīśabda Nāgarāja, Suvarṇaprabha Nāgarāja, Suvarṇavarṇa Nāgarāja, Kṛṣṇamukha Nāgarāja, Mahāmeghadhara Nāgarāja, Mahāsāgara Nāgarāja,
Kiḷāpa Nāgarāja, Brahma Nāgarāja, Priyadarśana Nāgarāja, Elāpattra Nāgarāja, and Dāpī Nāgarāja.
The Nāga King Rāvaṇa, the Nāga King Gaṅgā, the Nāga King Sindhu, the Nāga King Vakṣu, the Nāga King Sītā,
the Nāga King Guṇavanta, the Nāga King Anavatapta, the Nāga King Pāṃśula, the Nāga King Manuṣya,
the Nāga King Amanuṣya, the Nāga King Manuṣyamukha, the Nāga King Śiva, and the Nāga King Puṇya.
The Naga King Yama, the Naga King Vaiśravaṇa, the Naga King Śaṅkha, the Yellow Naga King, the Naga King Nanda,
the Naga King Upananda, the Naga King Virūḍhaka, the Naga King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the Naga King Virūpākṣa, the Naga King Vaiśravaṇa, and the Naga King Pañcaśikha.
The Naga King Ravana, the Naga King Manasvin, and other such naga kings—
desiring to hear and receive the Mahayana sutras, and having heard them, desiring to extensively proclaim and analyze them for the sake of all beings;
desiring to uphold the true Dharma and protect the true Dharma.

For the sake of protecting the Dharma, he firmly maintained the prohibitive precepts and bore the heavy burden of the Dharma—also rising from meditative concentration in the early morning, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, joined his palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were thirty-six thousand yakṣa kings, whose names were: the Yakṣa King Vaiśravaṇa, the Yakṣa King Ākāśa, the Yakṣa King Priyadarśana, the Yakṣa King Viśiṣṭadatta, the Yakṣa King Mahāratnakeyūravibhūṣita, the Yakṣa King Ekākṣa, the Yakṣa King Mahīprakampaka, the Yakṣa King Sumāla, the Yakṣa King Sukuladeva, the Yakṣa King Maṇibhadra, the Yakṣa King Pūrṇanagara, the Yakṣa King Padmaprabha, the Yakṣa King Cakravedika, and the Yakṣa King Mahāsamudravijaya.

These yakṣa kings, who followed the path of practice of Tathāgata Akṣobhya and had received and upheld the prohibitive precepts for the sake of protecting the True Dharma, likewise arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed their acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were forty-nine thousand *garuḍa* kings, whose names were: the *garuḍa* king Equal Strength Fragrant Elephant, the *garuḍa* king Firm Resolve, the *garuḍa* king Drum Sound, the *garuḍa* king Destroyer of All Dragon Kings’ Power, the *garuḍa* king Fire Light, the *garuḍa* king Spotted Wings, the *garuḍa* king Wheel Face, the *garuḍa* king Evil Nature, the *garuḍa* king Destroyer of the Family of the *nāga* King Vaśavartin, the *garuḍa* king Great Joy Destroyer of Vaśavartin’s Family, the *garuḍa* king True Vision, the *garuḍa* king Delightful Speech Great Compassion, the *garuḍa* king Dharma Joy, and the *garuḍa* king Gold-Wing Love.

These and other such kings of the garuḍas—none of whom possessed pride or negligence, all of whom had attained a heart that cherishes and protects the Mahāyāna, and who guarded the true Dharma of all Buddhas—also arose from meditative concentration in the early morning and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, and circumambulated him three times to the right. Having completed these acts of respect, they withdrew and sat to one side.

Furthermore, there were sixty-eight thousand gandharva kings, namely: the Gandharva King Joy, the Gandharva King Sovereign Song, the Gandharva King Present Love, the Gandharva King Attained by the Bull King, the Gandharva King Cloud-Enveloping, the Gandharva King Jīvajīvaka, and the Gandharva King Renowned Fame.

These and other gandharva kings likewise arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed their acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were ninety-eight thousand kinnara kings, namely: the Kinnara King Sudarśana, the Kinnara King Dīrghanāsa, the Kinnara King Ākarṣitacitta, the Kinnara King Bhāryāpriya, the Kinnara King Kleśavidhvamsaka, the Kinnara King Arivighātaka, the Kinnara King Mārakanyāpriya, the Kinnara King Mārakulavidhvamsaka, the Kinnara King Prajñāgarbha, the Kinnara King Gambhīranetra, the Kinnara King Viśuddhāryaguṇa, the Kinnara King Vinītendriya, and the Kinnara King Dūradarśin.

These and other kings of the kiṃnaras likewise arose from meditative concentration at dawn, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were eighteen thousand rākṣasa kings, namely: the rākṣasa king Bhasmaka (Ash-Burner), the rākṣasa king Mahiṣaśiras (Buffalo-Head), the rākṣasa king Piṅgakeśa (Yellow-Haired), the rākṣasa king Viṣamadaṃṣṭra (Uneven-Toothed), the rākṣasa king Kapālaśrotra (Skull-Eared), the rākṣasa king Madhulubdha (Honey-Greedy), the rākṣasa king Madhuvanna (Honey-Colored), the rākṣasa king Mahāgrīva (Large-Necked), the rākṣasa king Mahāpāna (Great-Drinker), the rākṣasa king Keśasaṃvṛtadeha (Body-Covered-with-Hair), the rākṣasa king Mahābala (Great-Strength), and the rākṣasa king Bhīṣaṇavarṇa (Frightful-Complexioned).

These rākṣasa kings—all of whom had severed the notion of being rākṣasas and whose minds were exclusively disciplined through the Mahāyāna—also arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were thirty-eight thousand *dānava* kings, whose names were: the *dānava* king Elephant Face, the *dānava* king Tusk, the *dānava* king Limb-Foot, the *dānava* king Donkey-Voice, the *dānava* king Flower-Ear, the *dānava* king Jewel-Ear, the *dānava* king Mouse-Catcher, the *dānava* king Fox-Catcher, the *dānava* king Weasel-Doubt, the *dānava* king Monkey-Face, and the *dānava* king Moon-Face.

These and other Dānava kings likewise arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.
Furthermore, there were seventy-eight thousand kumbhāṇḍa kings, whose names were Elephant-Ear Kumbhāṇḍa King, Winnowing-Basket-Ear Kumbhāṇḍa King, and Great-Fat Kumbhāṇḍa King.

These and other kumbhāṇḍa kings had all already abandoned the perception of being kumbhāṇḍas. Also, rising from meditative concentration in the early morning, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed their acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.
Furthermore, there were thirty-eight thousand kings of hungry ghosts, whose names were King Lightning Radiance, King Great Charity, King Admired by All, King Arrow, and King Ocean Waves.
All such kings as these—each and every one of them—delighted in the Mahāyāna sūtras and protected the True Dharma;
they constantly proclaimed and analyzed [the teachings] extensively for the sake of sentient beings;
they thirsted for the Mahāyāna, hungered for the Mahāyāna, and yearned for the Mahāyāna, adorning themselves solely with the Mahāyāna.

He constantly made the vow: "May I attain the precepts and attain wisdom. Furthermore, at dawn, he would arise from meditative concentration and proceed to where the Buddha was; there, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, joined his palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were eighty-eight thousand asura kings, namely: the asura king Vemacitra, the asura king Pūraṇa, the asura king Smṛtirāṣṭra, the asura king Viṣṇuśuddhagaṅgā, the asura king Śivakṣema, the asura king Gajagala, the asura king Triśṛṅgaparvata, the asura king Dhūmraśikha, the asura king Mahāduṣṭasvabhāva, and the asura king Tejodhvaja.

These and other asura kings—all of whom had completely abandoned their asura conceits, whose minds were disciplined, who were forever free from arrogance, and devoid of negligence—also arose from meditative concentration in the early morning and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, and circumambulated him three times to the right. Having completed these acts of respect, they withdrew and sat to one side.

Furthermore, there were sixty-five thousand great sovereigns of divine spells (*mahā-mantra-rāja*), whose names were: the Sovereign of Jewel Retention, the Sovereign of Inexhaustible Intent, the Sovereign of Inexhaustible Wealth, the Unobstructed Sovereign, and the Non-confrontational Sovereign.

These and other such great kings of mantras—those who cherish and revere the Mahāyāna, delight in expounding the Mahāyāna, protect the Mahāyāna, thirst for and yearn for the Mahāyāna, and crave and admire the Mahāyāna;
those who have attained Mahāyāna samādhi and are endowed with impartial conduct;

those who constantly desire to sever all doubt and, for the sake of protecting the True Dharma, uphold the pure precepts—they likewise arose from meditative concentration at dawn, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of veneration, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were ninety-nine thousand five hundred seers possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), whose names were: the seer Nārada, the seer Raibhya, the seer Vāmadeva, the seer Sunu, the seer Garga, the seer Sukra, the seer Aṅgāraka, the seer Mṛgaśṛṅga, the seer Mṛgākṣa, the seer Vigatamāna, the seer Vasiṣṭha, the seer Nandika, the seer Pañcaskandha, the seer Kalpādya, the seer Mahāmeghavarṇavastra, the seer Divyavastra, the seer Kauśika, the seer Phalada, the seer Nāgaruta, the seer Guṇaprāpta, the seer Māṃsaccheda, and the seer Sarvajīvitapradāna.

These and other rishis possessing the five supernormal powers likewise arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, and circumambulated him three times to the right. Having completed these acts of respect, they withdrew and sat to one side.

Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with immeasurable and innumerable gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, also rose from meditative concentration at dawn, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, the Four Heavenly Kings also arose from their meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there was King Prasenajit, the ruler of Śrāvastī, who, together with various minor kings, arrayed the fourfold army. These kings—those who cherished the Mahāyāna, delighted in proclaiming the Mahāyāna, and thirsted for the Mahāyāna;

those who, for the sake of protecting the True Dharma, had received and maintained the pure precepts—also arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit on one side.
Furthermore, there were fifty-three thousand great householders, including Sudatta and others, who all received the five precepts and resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
they cherished the Mahāyāna, thirsted for the Mahāyāna, and yearned for the Mahāyāna;
and in order to protect the Mahāyāna, they undertook and maintained the pure precepts.

For the sake of sentient beings, he followed after Bodhi—also rising from meditative concentration in the early morning, proceeding to where the Buddha was, prostrating with his head at the Buddha's feet, joining his palms in reverence, circumambulating him three times to the right; having completed these acts of veneration, he withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, there was a ruler of the kingdom of Campā named Candrapāla, who, together with various minor kings—all of whom observed the five precepts and had all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—also rose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of veneration, withdrew to sit to one side.
Furthermore, there are sixteen great kingdoms:

the kingdom of Aṅga, the kingdom of Magadha, the kingdom of Kāśi, the kingdom of Kośala, the kingdom of Vṛji, the kingdom of Malla, the kingdom of Bhadra, the kingdom of Suma, the kingdom of Ama, the kingdom of Avanti, the kingdom of Kuru, the kingdom of Pañcāla, the kingdom of Vatsa, the kingdom of Śūrasena, the kingdom of Yavana, and the kingdom of Kamboja.

In this way, all sentient beings within these sixteen great kingdoms all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, rising from meditative concentration at dawn, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, and circumambulated him three times to the right. Having completed these acts of veneration, they withdrew to sit on one side.

Furthermore, Lady Mallikā, together with sixteen thousand ladies, also rose from meditative concentration in the early morning and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of veneration, withdrew to sit on one side.

Furthermore, there were eighteen thousand *upāsikās*, including Viśākhā and others—all of whom had resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, who delighted in the Mahāyāna and thirsted for the Mahāyāna, who upheld the pure precepts in order to protect the True Dharma, who cultivated the path to *bodhi* in order to gather and assist the dharmas of the Unsurpassed Way, and who had all attained the mind of non-retrogression—yet manifested in female bodies for the sake of delivering sentient beings and always delighted in proclaiming the Mahāyāna sūtras. At dawn, they also arose from meditative concentration and went to where the Buddha was; they prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed their acts of respect, withdrew to sit on one side.

Furthermore, there was the Devaputra Īśvara, accompanied by immeasurable hosts of devas, who manifested great supernatural transformations and emitted light of five colors; the various flowers he held were as vast as Mount Sumeru.

That is to say: the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, fragrant flowers, great fragrant flowers, exquisite flowers, great exquisite flowers, lovely-to-behold flowers, greatly lovely-to-behold flowers, seasonal flowers, perennial flowers, *mandārava* flowers, and *mahāmandārava* flowers;
as well as various incenses, namely sandalwood incense, flower incense, and *bhṛṅgaka* incense, along with various musical instruments;
and furthermore, they carried various flowers as large as chariot wheels.

Again, rising from meditative concentration at dawn, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, joined his palms in reverence, and circumambulated him three times to the right. Having completed these acts of respect, he withdrew and sat to one side.

Furthermore, there were Brahmās such as Śikhin and others, accompanied by immeasurable Brahmās, who emitted five-colored light; this light was able to destroy the greed and darkness of all sentient beings on Vulture Peak.
Carrying various incenses, mixed flowers, and musical instruments, they came to the place where the Buddha was.
In the great city of Rājagṛha, at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, the ground measured a full yojana in length and breadth;
it was completely covered with celestial garments, leaving no empty space between them—namely, Kauśika robes, Kalinga robes, kṣauma robes, and kauśeya robes.
He further spread out lion thrones made of the seven precious gems, each throne being one million and eight thousand yojanas high.
Having established these offerings, he circumambulated the Tathāgata thirty times to the right, removed the jeweled robes from his body to cover the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, for the sake of all sentient beings, shall rain down the rain of Dharma."
At that time, a great voice resounded again from the midst of the void:
"World-Honored One!
Although all sentient beings have heard of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, they are unable to understand them. We only pray that the Tathāgata will expound and explain them."
Furthermore, there were immeasurable goose-kings, such as the Lion Goose King and others, who brought various kinds of flowers, incense, and offering implements to worship the precious lion throne.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable peacock kings, such as the peacock king Supakṣa and others, who brought various fragrant flowers and exquisite music to make offerings to the Buddha.

There were also immeasurable cuckoo kings (*kukila*), such as the king Sucarita and others, who likewise arose from their meditative concentration at dawn, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of veneration, withdrew to sit on one side.

Furthermore, the king of the kalavinka birds from the Snowy Mountains, the Lotus King, and others, carrying various incenses and flowers, also arose from meditative concentration in the early morning and proceeded to where the Buddha was. They prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of veneration, withdrew to sit at one side.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable kings of jīvajīvaka birds, such as the Unobstructed King and others, who also arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable mountain kings, with Mount Sumeru as their foremost, who also rose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of respect, withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were the kings of medicinal herbs from Mount Gandhamādana, such as Kṣāntirāja and others, who also arose from meditative concentration in the early morning, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having completed these acts of veneration, withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, all trees constantly produced flowers and fruits;
and all musical instruments, without being struck or touched, spontaneously gave forth subtle and wondrous sounds.
At that time, all the lions and various predatory beasts within the Snowy Mountains regarded one another with a heart of loving-kindness, as a mother regards her child;
furthermore, all mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous insects attained a heart of loving-kindness, regarding each other as their only son;
and so it was likewise for all the malevolent birds.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of venomous snakes—namely, those whose gaze is poisonous, those whose breath is poisonous, those whose bite is poisonous, and those whose touch is poisonous—and they too attain a mind of loving-kindness;
likewise, it is the same for the sixteen kinds of evil disciplines (an-ārya-vṛtti), such that all these evil sentient beings fully receive the five precepts.

At that time, the entire great assembly collectively undertook and maintained the practice of pure precepts; they delighted in hearing and receiving the Mahāyāna sūtras, revering the Mahāyāna and protecting the Mahāyāna;
and toward those who reviled or slandered the Mahāyāna sūtras, they looked upon them with reproach, while showing reverence, respect, and making offerings to those who upheld them.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Secret Treasury rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated before the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This great assembly all harbors doubts.
I now wish to ask a question; I only pray that you will grant me leave.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family, I am now able to dispel the doubts in this assembly; ask whatever you wish.”
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ghanameghagarbha said:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice so as to attain dhāraṇī?”
How can one attain the Samādhi of the Great Ocean?
How can one understand the true speech of all Buddhas?
How can one come to know the fullness of the flavor of the Dharma?
How can one perceive the subtle and secret treasury?
How can one enter the place of peace and security, and also behold the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding?
How can one obtain the Tathāgata’s precious treasury and forever sever the poverty and suffering of sentient beings?
How can one understand the profound meaning of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas?
How can one reach the further shore of the great ocean of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas?
How does a Bodhisattva enter the realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas?
How does a bodhisattva protect and uphold all the illusory dharmas of the Buddhas?
How does a bodhisattva attain the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, and having attained it, how is he able to expound it?
How is he able to know the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)?
“How does one obtain the body of the Buddha-sun, the body of the moon, and the body of the comet?
How does one reach the ultimate limit of the Tathāgatas?
How can one attain the pure karma of all Buddhas?”
How does one attain that which is practiced by the Tathāgata?
How does one obtain the Buddha’s profound and pure pool?
How does one obtain the Buddha’s Puṇḍarīka flower?
How does one attain the sovereign power of the Buddhas?
How can one obtain the wealth of all Buddhas?
How can one perceive the true mark of the Tathāgata?
How is it that one sees the Buddha as eternally abiding and unchanging?
How can one obtain the golden body of a Tathāgata?
How does a bodhisattva become a Dharma-king of the Buddhas?
How can one attain the vajra-dharmakāya?
How can one attain the Buddha’s eternal body and eternal voice?
"How does a bodhisattva reach the place where the Tathāgata dwells, yet remain without the notion of dwelling?"
How is it that seeing the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, as eternal, blissful, self, and pure does not constitute a wrong view?
And what are the Tathāgata’s true birth-body and true dharma-body?
How is it that the Tathāgata possesses a vajra-body and destroys the composite body?
How is it that seeing the destruction of the body is called true vision?
How is it that the body of the Tathāgata is not said to be established by flesh, blood, sinews, and bones, even if such a body exists?
"What is the view of emptiness?
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, how can there be anything obtained?
How is it that when he teaches the Dharma, all who hear it hear the Dharma of non-attainment, as if nothing at all exists?"
How, moreover, can one speak of the Tathāgata as truly eternal?
How does he enter nirvāṇa, or not enter nirvāṇa?
What is called the precept of truthful speech, if there is neither purity nor defilement?
How can one praise those who uphold the precepts?
If the Buddha-dharma were not to perish, why speak of the extinction of the Dharma?
Furthermore, you say that at the time of the Dharma's extinction, there will be many who violate the prohibitions.
If the Tathāgata’s buddha-nature is pure, supremely pure, and ultimately pure, such being its nature,
why would one delight in birth and death?
And why do the bodhisattvas always speak of the joy of birth and death?
What is the nature of the Tathāgata that bodhisattvas delight in beholding?
What is the permanence of afflictions?
And what is the craving for afflictions?
How, furthermore, can one enter the gateway of all afflictions?
How can one cultivate the deeds of all buddha-fields?
How can one come to thoroughly know the root of affliction?
"How do bodhisattvas skillfully attain the eradication of the doubts they have raised regarding the Buddha, such that they possess a mind of permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
If they are free from doubt, why would they fear birth and death?"
If one fears birth and death, how can one again find delight and attachment?
How can one attain the Buddha-way?
How can one turn the wheel of Dharma?
How does one deliver sentient beings, knowing that the Buddha-nature is never severed?
How does one subdue the hosts of Māra, causing them to leave the realm of Māra?
How does one deliver sentient beings from the great ocean of suffering of birth and death?
How does one speak of birth and death, and how does one guide others along the path of birth and death?
How does one reach the immeasurable great ocean of birth and death?
How does one seek birth and death, and yearn for the path of birth and death?
Why is it that one craves birth and death, being stingy and unwilling to let go?
How can one open the gates of birth and death like a *puṇḍarīka* lotus?
Why are the fetters of affliction like the four great oceans?
How is it that all afflictions constantly arise as if they were making a vow?
"How does one obtain the mind of hell?
How does one constantly seek the mind of hell?"
How does one cultivate and accumulate the precepts that lead to hell?
How do the karmic actions leading to hell and the body of hell increase and flourish?
By means of swords, arrows, spears, axes, wheels, and fire, how can one destroy the fruits of hell for sentient beings?
How does one bring peace and happiness to the sentient beings in the hells?
How can one pour down great rain to extinguish the fires of hell?
How can one dwell within hell without undergoing its retribution?
How does one act as a ship’s captain for those in hell?
How does one act as a great panacea for those in hell?
And how is it possible to block the path to the hells?
"How does one create the lamp of wisdom to destroy the darkness of birth and death?
How can one dwell within birth and death without being defiled by the poisons of affliction?
Though abiding in non-abiding, one does not abide in emptiness; "
They are able to eliminate all afflictions, just as the sun shines upon the snow;
they perceive the Tathāgata as permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
their minds abide securely, like Mount Sumeru.
Immovable and unchanging, like the banner of Śakra;
the Tathāgata is not, in reality, ultimately in parinirvāṇa;
yet it is also said that the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa, for his mind is indestructible, just like a diamond.
"How does one attain a sense of shame and dread of blame?
How does one obtain a fine body?
And how can one further obtain a body that is loved and respected by all?"
How does one attain non-attachment?
How does one attain non-aversion?
And how can one attain subtle and wondrous radiance?
How does one attain the state of correctness?
How does one attain mastery?
"And how can one obtain a great assembly of followers?"
How can one obtain an unbreakable retinue?
By being neither regressive nor losing [one's resolve], by not craving food and drink;
by constantly cultivating contentment and never eating meat.
Toward all sentient beings, he constantly gives rise to a heart of affection;
he is always revered by the world, receiving the name "Lord of All Great Generosity";
he receives the name "Great Power," and receives the name "Vigorous Practice."

Possessing great loving-kindness, great compassion, great equanimity, great joy, and the dhāraṇī of great wisdom, they accord with the world, bring peace to the world, and bring happiness to the world.
"How does one attain that which is unsurpassed in the world, peerless in the world, and boundless in the world?
By constantly practicing right speech, cultivating the holy life (brahmacarya),
practicing the conduct of great compassion, and joyfully performing noble deeds."
Seeing the empty realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they teach in accordance with it;
seeing the non-empty realm, they teach in the same way;
teaching the characteristics of the Buddha-dharma, they perceive the true Dharma of the Buddha.

Having attained the wealth of pure and sovereign morality, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of Dharma, and the wealth that does not decay, one becomes a treasury of wealth for impoverished sentient beings.
For the sake of all sentient beings, one attains the three samādhis—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and desiring to be born in a pure land, one attains a body according to one's vows.
Although he assumes this aggregate body for the sake of sentient beings, he does not seek any reward of gratitude from them;
he praises the observance of precepts and censures those who break them;
and he cannot be thwarted or corrupted by the various heterodoxies.
"Though he studies non-Buddhist scriptures, he does not follow their doctrines; the words and meanings of the Dharma he teaches are never interrupted.
Though he bears the names of śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, he ultimately never gives rise to the notion of being a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa;
though he is proficient in mathematics and incantations, his mind has never once harbored a thought of craving or attachment."

Although they manifest entering temples of the devas to offer worship, respect, reliance, and prostrations for the sake of sentient beings, their inner minds always abide in accordance with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
They manifest the practice of the ten non-virtues while being, in reality, practitioners of the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), protected by all Buddhas as if looking upon an only son;

they are well able to protect and uphold the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas, can turn the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas, and deeply perceive the profound Dharma-realm and the true aspect of all Buddhas.
The practices they cultivate are equal to those of all Buddhas; they attain immeasurable bodies and immeasurable activities.
They skillfully understand all the secret speech of the Buddhas and eliminate pride just as the Buddhas do.
They skillfully expound the profound and secret meaning of the dharma-realm; though they speak of pride, they harbor no thought of pride, nor do they instruct others to give rise to pride.
The mind is free from greed, anger, delusion, and fear, just like that of all Buddhas;

its conduct is immeasurable, its subtle mysteries are immeasurable, all dharmas are immeasurable, its eloquence is immeasurable, its nature and characteristics are immeasurable, and its reality is immeasurable;
it perceives the true, perceives the real, perceives the nature, and perceives the dharmas.

"For the sake of severing the afflictions of all sentient beings, I expound the Dharma, so that they may constantly know and see the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and forever cross the great ocean of the fetters of affliction.

For the sake of delivering sentient beings, I preach the Dharma for crossing the ocean of the fetters of affliction: that those who have not yet crossed may cross; those who have not yet been delivered, may be delivered; those who have not yet been delivered, have been delivered, or will be delivered; those who have not yet attained liberation, have attained liberation, or will attain liberation; those who have not yet attained peace, have attained peace, or will attain peace; and those who have not yet entered Nirvana, may attain Nirvana."
"Having personally realized the Dharma-realm, he clearly perceives its true reality;
yet for the sake of sentient beings, he speaks of both the real and the unreal.
Having already destroyed the four Māras throughout immeasurable kalpas, he manifests his presence beneath the Bodhi tree to subdue the hosts of Māra for the sake of sentient beings."
Internally, he possesses true knowledge and vision, having long since defeated all Māras; yet for the sake of sentient beings, he proclaims that he is now destroying them.
By means of skillful expedients, he turns the wheel of Dharma; by means of skillful expedients, he manifests entry into nirvana.
"How can one attain the supernormal powers of all Buddhas?
How can one become a Dharma King, a Tathāgata Buddha?
How can one attain the subtle and secret Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas?"
How does one attain the inconceivable state of a Buddha?
How is it possible to attain the immeasurable, the ineffable, the incalculable, the unsurpassed, and the boundless qualities of all Buddhas?
"How can one bestow upon all sentient beings the ambrosial flavor of the Dharma?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Secret Treasury, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Noble son! The question you have now asked is most excellent and skillful.
You have raised this inquiry because you desire to bring peace and happiness to the sentient beings of the world."
"All sentient beings are blinded by ignorance and are unable to know the true merits possessed by all Buddhas. 'Good son!

You now desire that all sentient beings may fully obtain the eye of wisdom, the eternal eye, and eternal light, so that they may forever cross the great river of birth, death, and afflictions, and thoroughly understand the bodhi-practices of all Buddhas;'"
Desiring to shatter the cocoon of the fetters of ignorance for all sentient beings, he demonstrates and guides them toward the practice of unsurpassed bodhi.
All sentient beings constantly delight in preaching impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity;

yet now, he wishes to reveal permanence, bliss, self, and purity. While the Tathāgata ultimately enters parinirvāṇa—characterized by impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity—[he reveals the true nature].
Now, I wish to reveal that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not undergo ultimate extinction, but abide eternally and remain unchanging. "Good son!
All sentient beings constantly give rise to false discriminations within the Dharma-realm;
Yet the nature of the dharma-realm is truly without discrimination.
You now wish to inquire into the meaning of non-discrimination; for this reason, you have posed your question. Good son!

All sentient beings are constantly defiled by the poisons of perversion; the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is a great and skilled physician. It is your wish that the Tathāgata, the King of Physicians, should proclaim mantras and bestow medicines to cure their sufferings.

“Good son! Just as the brahmin Cāṇakya, the Nirgranthas, and other brahmins truly were not arhats yet conceived the notion that they were arhats; they were not noble ones yet conceived the notion that they were noble ones; they were not devas yet conceived the notion that they were devas;
and they truly did not possess the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, yet they conceived the notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

You now wish to extract the poisonous arrows of heterodoxy for such sentient beings, to untie their heterodox bonds, shatter their heterodox prisons, and release them from their heterodox nets; you wish to bestow the flavor of the Dharma, feed them with ambrosia, settle them in repose within the four dhyānas, and anoint them with the fragrance of pure precepts.
With the four immeasurables as flowers and a sense of shame and remorse as clothing, he therefore asked this question:
"Good son! All sentient beings do not know the general characteristics, nor do they know the specific characteristics."

Characteristics, absence of characteristics, neither characteristics nor absence of characteristics; the characteristic of non-characteristic, the characteristic of non-absence-of-characteristic; unknowable, yet not unknowable;
neither this nor that, neither hand nor finger, neither this, nor that, nor the middle.
It is neither created nor uncreated; neither shown nor unshown; neither caused nor uncaused; neither blinking nor not blinking; neither known nor known by wisdom;
neither consciousness nor known by consciousness;
neither abiding nor non-abiding; neither darkness nor light; neither sign nor name; neither light nor heavy; neither weak nor strong; neither a place nor a non-place; neither pure nor impure.
It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither existent nor non-existent; neither expressible nor inexpressible;
neither grasped nor abandoned; neither arising nor ceasing; neither real nor unreal; neither correct nor erroneous.
It is neither ultimate nor non-ultimate; it is neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit; it is neither time nor non-time; it is neither purifiable nor unpurifiable;
it is neither an agent nor capable of acting; it is neither arising nor ceasing; it is neither cold nor hot;
it is neither the aggregates, sense-bases, nor elements; it is neither the cause of fetters nor the cause of karma; it is neither birth nor falling away; it is neither long nor increasing.
It is not that there is falling away, for it is ultimately without falling;
it is not a conditioned phenomenon, for it has forever severed all forms of existence;
it is neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present.
Neither real nor unreal, neither having a nature nor lacking a nature;
neither form, nor sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
neither exhausted nor unexhausted, yet incapable of being exhausted.
It is neither equal nor unequal, and there is nothing with which it can be compared;
it is not earth, water, fire, or wind.
"In the entire dharma-realm, there is truly no body;"
The characteristic of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is ultimately and truly real; this is called the Tathāgata.

Accomplished through immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable great merits, such a body is precisely the true Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas; its meaning is profoundly deep and inconceivable.

The Dharma-realm of the Tathāgata is profound, subtle, and far-reaching; without departing from its original place, it proclaims the True Dharma, which all Buddhas of the ten directions hear and know. Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata acts through the power of sovereign spiritual mastery, such profound speech is not heard by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. "Good son,
for what reason do the Buddhas not speak for them so that they might hear it?"

Good son! Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not understand the meaning of even a single word; they are like those born blind, like people who have drunk poison and gone mad, like silkworms within their cocoons, like those struck by a poisoned arrow, or like those afflicted with phlegm-dyspepsia.
For this reason, the Buddhas do not speak of it. "Good son!

All sentient beings are constantly afflicted by the diseases of the various fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*). The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, can bestow the medicine of the Dharma; using wondrous incantations and arts, they extract their poisoned arrows and remove the cataracts of their skin. Yet sentient beings truly do not know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging. Therefore, the Tathāgata kindles the lamp of the wisdom-Dharma, enabling them all to perceive the permanence, bliss, self, and purity."
For example, when the sun rises, it causes all sentient beings to universally perceive the various features of the great earth, such as its elevations and depressions;

so too is it with the Tathāgata. All sentient beings do not know the Vaipulya [sūtras], nor can they attain the dhāraṇī-samādhi; they do not know the timing of the Buddha, nor the wealth of the Buddha; they do not see the Buddha’s body, nor do they understand the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa; they do not know whether the Buddha-dharma will perish or not, yet they claim that the Tathāgata is impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity, possessing the arrows of affliction, and being like food mixed with poison. Therefore, for the sake of such people, I proclaim the permanence, bliss, self, and purity of all Buddhas, desiring to remove the darkness of ignorance from these individuals.
“Good son! Excellent, excellent!
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have never before heard the meaning of even this single syllable; it is because you now wish to enable them to hear it that you have posed this question.”
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
There is a Great Vaipulya Sūtra King of Ambrosia, which opens the great treasury of jewels to provide for the poor and destitute, and reveals the storehouse of the merits of all Buddhas.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; this nature is inexhaustible, though it has been hidden since the past, and now it is sought to be manifested.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, kindle the great lamp of wisdom, causing all sentient beings to see with perfect clarity.
Son of good family!
I am about to speak; you should now pose your question, in accordance with the vows you have made since long ago.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Secret Treasury said:
“World-Honored One!

From the past until now, I truly had no such aspiration. It is solely due to the World-Honored One’s great compassion, kindness, and the power of his supernormal faculties that he has caused me to pose this question for the sake of delivering sentient beings—desiring to shatter their poverty and suffering, and to ensure that the resolve of all sentient beings remains inexhaustible.”

What the Tathāgata now teaches can extinguish the great darkness of ignorance of all sentient beings and enable them to obtain the treasure of wisdom; it causes all sentient beings to clearly perceive the Buddha-nature and to realize the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
The meaning of what you have now asked is exceedingly profound.

It is for the sake of delivering sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death; for the sake of widely disseminating the Vaipulya sutras; for the sake of the eternal Dharma; and to bestow upon all the flavor of the nectar of the Dharma, thereby severing the suffering of poverty among sentient beings.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain this for you so that all sentient beings may attain peace and happiness;
you, now, should skillfully uphold this meaning for the sake of all sentient beings.

"Good son! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpannas, Sugatas, Lokavidas, Anuttaras, Puruṣadamyasārathis, Śāstṛs of gods and humans, Buddhas, and Bhagavats possess a single dharma called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). By means of this Dharma-realm, the Buddha-Bhagavats possess eternal wisdom;

with the water of this eternal wisdom, they purify themselves by bathing, partake of the flavor of nectar (*amṛta*), and bestow it as a gift upon all sentient beings while cultivating and accumulating all that is practiced by the Buddhas. You should now partake of this flavor of nectar."
"Once you have taken this medicine, you must further bestow it upon others.

I shall now speak; listen well. My words are excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end. Their meaning is true, their phrasing is skillful, and their tone is pure. They are entirely unadulterated, fully embodying the characteristics of the pure and holy life of a brahmacārin."
The Mahāvaipulya Amogha-saṃkalpa Sūtra, Scroll One.
The Mahāvaipulya Amogha-saṃkalpa Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
The Great Cloud Sūtra, First Division, Remainder of the Chapter on the Great Assembly’s Prowess: “Good son!
There is the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the ocean of dhāraṇīs and the ocean of samādhis.”
The Dharma-seal of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-city of all Buddhas;
the Dharma-realm is profoundly deep, eternally abiding and unchanging;
it is inconceivable, characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

"World-Honored One!..."
In the Mahāyāna sūtras, how many kinds of samādhis, dhāraṇīs, secret treasuries of the path to be practiced, and unhindered eloquence in joyful exposition are there?
Furthermore, how many kinds of Tathāgata-realms and world-systems are there?

The Tathāgata possesses great compassion and pities all beings; therefore, I venture to ask this question today. I pray that the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings will take pity on me and explain it.
“Having spoken thus, I shall receive and uphold it with the highest reverence.
At that time, there was a son of heaven named Akṣayamati who, within the great assembly, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses for the sake of Brahmā:
“Excellent, Great Brahmā King, Who asks the Buddha about the meaning of reality.
The Buddha shall answer according to reality, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
You should listen with a sincere heart, revering and honoring it;
for in each and every Vaipulya Sūtra, meanings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are difficult to comprehend.
The Tathāgata, the Great Dharma King, extensively expounds the Dharma-realm;
the Buddha has attained the dharma of dhāraṇī, which is not understood by those of the two vehicles. "O Mahābrahmā!
The meaning of the Mahāyāna sūtras is not merely of one kind, but extends even to ten thousand kinds.

Even if there were a person whose wisdom equaled that of Ānanda and whose lifespan lasted as long as the sands of the Ganges River, they would be unable to receive, uphold, and fully comprehend their principles and meanings.
Furthermore, suppose this person possesses such sharp eloquence that their speech is as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; even so, they could not exhaustively explain it.

Why is this? Because the meaning of this Mahāyāna sūtra is profound, inconceivable, immeasurable, and its realm difficult to know. Even all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present cannot exhaustively explain its phrases and meanings.
"Brahmā! Just as a physician, for the sake of treating illnesses, cannot exhaustively describe all medicinal prescriptions,
so too it is with the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
Brahmā! It is like a woman who has but one son; wishing for him to grow up, she gradually gives him ghee to consume. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are also like this.
“Since Brahmā has already raised this question for the sake of sentient beings, I shall listen to its meaning with a sincere mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Secret Treasury addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"In this sutra, four hundred samādhis are taught; their meaning is exceedingly profound and difficult to comprehend. I only pray that the Tathāgata will analyze and explain them.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"

“Good son! Regarding what you have asked—desiring to heal the various evils, defilements, and impurities of sentient beings so that they may attain a mind of patience and right faith, a mind of right diligence, mindfulness, and concentration; and desiring that those of meager merit in the future may give rise to merit—you have therefore raised this question.”

“Good son! In whatever country, city, town, or village the fourfold assembly receives, upholds, recites, copies, and explains a sūtra such as this, if there is drought, rain shall fall; once the rain has fallen, it shall cease.”
"Good son! In whatever land sentient beings may uphold, recite, copy, explain, or listen to this sutra, you should know that such persons shall attain a vajra-body."
Why is this? Because within this sutra there is a divine mantra.
For the sake of sentient beings, all Buddhas of the three periods of time have together proclaimed it:
“Ukyau lei, moukyau lei, toudi, bitoudi, dani jiedi, danna raidi, danna sengtaxi. If there are members of the fourfold assembly who read and recite this mantra, they shall be praised by all Buddhas.”

If there is a kingdom that wishes to pray for rain, on the days of the six fasts, its king should purify himself by bathing, make offerings to the Triple Gem, and with reverence and praise, invoke the names of the dragon kings.
"Good son! The nature of the four great elements may be made to change;
yet for it to be said that if one recites and upholds this mantra, the heavens would not send down rain—such a thing is impossible."
Regarding the meaning of the four hundred samādhis you previously asked about, listen attentively with a sincere mind;
I shall explain them for you. "Good son!

Within this sutra, there is the 'Great Ocean of Pure Water' Samādhi of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which is profound and cannot be known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; therefore, it is called 'profound. "
Because it can sever all birth-and-death and thirst, it is called "pure water";
because its limits cannot be found, it is called the "great ocean";
and because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are identical in their equality, it is called "samādhi."

If there is a bodhisattva who possesses these samādhis, they shall attain a body of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; they shall obtain an ocean of great learning and a treasure-trove of great learning; their bodhicitta shall remain unshakable; they shall possess the non-retrogressive body of the Buddha’s wisdom which is eternally abiding, without change, with a mind free from doubt or obstruction, never departing from the rain of Dharma, constantly encountering the Triple Gem, meeting with virtuous friends, and accomplishing all true and genuine merit.
"Good son! You should receive and uphold this samādhi.
Having upheld it, you will then fully accomplish immeasurable merits."

"Furthermore, good son! There is also the samādhi called 'Entering the Great Ocean of Profoundly Pure Water. No other samādhi can proclaim the characteristics of this samādhi; therefore, it is named 'profound.
It washes away birth and death; therefore, it is named 'water.'"
Because its bottom cannot be reached, it is called the "Great Ocean";
because one attains the immovable body and the permanence, bliss, self, and purity, it is called "entry";
because it is ultimate, it is called "samādhi."
"Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who possesses this samādhi, they can transform themselves into the forms of various devas.
When they see one who serves Brahmā, they immediately manifest as the image of Brahmā, yet they do so to dismantle the service of Brahmā while their mind remains unattached."
If one sees those who worship Īśvara, one manifests in the form of Īśvara;
if one sees those who worship the Eight-Armed One, one manifests in the form of the Eight-Armed One;
if one sees those who worship Khaṇḍa, one manifests in the form of Khaṇḍa.
Seeing those who worship celestial mothers, he manifests in the form of a celestial mother;
seeing those who worship spirits, he immediately manifests in the form of a spirit.
Although he displays such various forms and images to destroy their attachments, his mind is in truth free from all clinging.

When he sees a butcher, he immediately manifests in the form of a butcher; desiring to transform them so that they will refrain from killing, he likewise manifests in the forms of those at taverns or even as a *caṇḍāla*.
When he sees places of gambling, games of chance, or merriment, he manifests in their likeness in order to sever their poverty.

Though they manifest as having livestock, wives, children, slaves, and servants, their inner minds constantly cultivate the pure conduct (brahmacarya); even while wearing precious ornaments, their hearts remain ever pure.
He manifests the consumption of various sweet and delicious foods, yet internally he is always nourished and moistened by the joy of the Dharma.
He enters the quarters of courtesans in order to transform those who are driven by desire and evil, as well as all who are unwholesome.

The Bodhisattva manifests the bodies of physicians, diviners, and birds of prey, even down to all various species of animals; he likewise manifests as those with all manner of physical deformities and incomplete limbs, desiring to proclaim the faults and afflictions of the body;
and even manifesting in the likeness of the ninety-five kinds of heterodox paths, in order to shatter their views.
He manifests his own body with the four hundred and four diseases in order to cure the internal and external ailments of sentient beings;
he recites non-Buddhist texts and understands various languages.

He manifests the forms of slaves, servants, men, women, the young, and the old, as well as the manifestations of birth, aging, sickness, and death, desiring thereby to discipline and transform all sentient beings.
He is able to understand the languages of all birds, beasts, and other creatures, and manifests as fragrant incense, flowers, medicinal herbs, and fruits.

He may appear in the form of a king, a prince, a minister, or a householder; or he may manifest as a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa; or as the forms of Śakra Devendra, a Cakravartin King, the sun, the moon, and so forth.
He manifests as the Four Great Heavenly Kings because he desires to protect the four continents;
he manifests the sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas so that he never ultimately enters parinirvāṇa.
They manifest as various forms without destroying the nature of form.
Although they attain rebirth in the pure lands of all Buddhas, they ultimately do not discriminate between the characteristics of those lands.
They obtain the profound samādhis of all Buddhas, yet within the dharma-realm, they remain without discrimination.
As a lord of gods and men, his mind was free from arrogance.
Although he spoke of dream-events, he did not perceive the characteristics of dreams.
Though he manifested demonic activities externally, there was in reality no demonic karma.
Moving through the world, one is not defiled by worldly dharmas, just as a lotus flower remains unstained though it dwells in the mud.
Son of good family!
Such a fruit is called the accomplishment of the samādhi entered into the profound great ocean.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the assembly named Śubha who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Dharma of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep and secret; for the sake of all sentient beings, you have analyzed and expounded it."

Yet this Devadatta, of meager merit, dull faculties, and foolishness, did not listen nor accept [the teaching]; he was ignorant of the debt of gratitude and associated solely with the six groups of wicked bhikṣus, performing the same deeds as they. He increased his destiny in hell, shed the blood of the Buddha’s body, and brought about the schism of the Saṃgha.
Born of the Śākya clan, he has increased his arrogance; in truth, he is not human, yet we forcibly call him human. Examining his conduct and traces, he is no different from a beast.

Furthermore, for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* eons, they have constantly harbored malevolent and rebellious thoughts toward the Tathāgata; whatever they may give as offerings bears no fruit, and the wholesome deeds they themselves cultivate likewise do not reach fulfillment, being no different from those such as the Nirgranthas.
The Nirgranthas preach that there is no receiving and no giving; Devadatta is likewise the same—he is truly a partisan of Māra and not a follower of the Buddha.
Why is this? Because they constantly harbor harmful intentions toward the Tathāgata;
though they bear the name of śramaṇa, they lack the true meaning of a śramaṇa.
It is just like a bald man who wraps a sharp sword in a *kāṣāya* robe; he is truly a shaveling and is called "lifeless," and his followers are likewise so.
He is not truly the World-Honored One, yet they conceive of him as the World-Honored One.
World-Honored One, Tathāgata, if you are the Omniscient One, for what reason do you permit such a wicked person to leave the household life, shave his head, and receive full ordination?
The Tathāgata’s teachings are intended to cause all sentient beings to give rise to roots of goodness; why, then, does this person alone fail to do so?

Out of compassion, the Tathāgata constantly employs eloquent discourse to widely proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; those who hear it receive its nourishment, and their roots of goodness blossom forth.
Devadatta—why was he not included among those who receive these benefits?
The Tathāgata’s nature is pure, his body is pure, his mind is pure, and his retinue should be pure; why then are there such as these within the assembly?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmeghaghanagarbha, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, said to Śubhavyūha:
“Excellent, excellent!
Great Brahmin, none of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others have been able to inquire into this matter.”
It is well that you are now able to inquire about this meaning.
Listen attentively with a sincere mind!
I shall, relying upon the majestic spiritual power and the path-force of the Buddha, explain it extensively for you.
"You should not say that Devadatta was ungrateful. This man knew gratitude; it was not that he was ignorant of it.
Although he shared the same conduct as the group of six, this does not constitute evil."
Devadatta is inconceivable; the practices and deeds he cultivates are entirely identical to those of the Tathāgata.
The practices and deeds of the Tathāgata are precisely the practices and deeds of Devadatta.
All sentient beings are unable to reveal or manifest the true merits of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One;
Devadatta, however, can demonstrate them to others, enabling incalculable and immeasurable sentient beings to dwell securely in roots of goodness.
The karmic conduct of the Tathāgata does not belong to the seed-nature of hell; how then can you say that Devadatta is a person destined for hell?
You claim his actions are identical to those of the group of six.
"You should now know, Great Brahmin, that the group of six bhikṣus is not actually wicked, and the practices they perform are likewise identical to the Buddha’s practice."
The blood of the Tathāgata’s body truly does not flow out, nor could Devadatta cause it to flow out.
If one were to say that the shadow of a tree can bleed, such a thing is impossible.
The body of the Tathāgata is also like this.
If one says that blood flows from it, you should know that this is indeed a skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) and is inconceivable. Great Brahmin!
The lineage of Śākyamuni Tathāgata is as pure as deep blue lapis lazuli; among all his disciples, there are none who violate the prohibitions.
I likewise do not see any disciple of the Tathāgata who has broken the precepts.
The unsurpassed true Dharma taught by the Tathāgata truly causes those who hear it to give rise to roots of goodness; it is not that they do not do so.

The great assembly of the Tathāgata has accomplished the keeping of the precepts and has all entered the realm of the Buddha. His disciples and retinue are like a sandalwood forest, surrounded solely by sandalwood trees, such that they cannot be broken or destroyed, being like a mountain of vajra, and no one can be found capable of destroying them.
Those who possess fear can be destroyed;
the disciples of the Tathāgata are forever free from sorrow and fear. If they have no sorrow or fear, how could they be destroyed?
It is indestructible, like a pride of lions. The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, is like a lion king, with a retinue consisting purely of lions.
Such a retinue is difficult to fathom; it is not within the realm of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and it cannot be extinguished, like fire covered by ashes.
The Tathāgata, the unsurpassed one of all-knowledge, if he permits one to shave the head and receive full ordination, that person shall never violate the prohibitions.
All sentient beings enter the sphere of the Tathāgata’s knowledge; therefore, the Tathāgata is named "All-Knowing One."
Devadatta, being fully endowed with such qualities as these, cannot be called one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha.
"O Great Brahmin! Even if there were ten million immeasurable Māras, they likewise could not cause a schism."
If it is said that the wicked Devadatta has disrupted the Saṃgha, one should know that this is actually a skillful means; how then can it be said that his conduct is the same as that of animals?
Devadatta was truly born into the pure lineage of the Śākya Tathāgata; he was not born as an animal.
It is impossible that one born of the Śākya clan would commit such evils.
The evil deeds committed by Devadatta were intended to manifest the power of the merits of the Śākya Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is impossible that one born into the Śākya clan could be called a "shaven-headed man."
Devadatta was well able to protect and uphold the pure precepts of liberation; how then can he be called a Nirgrantha?
One who possesses evil desires is termed an "evil person," yet Devadatta’s mind was free from evil desire; how then can he be called an "evil bhikṣu"?
"One who practices the Tathāgata’s skillful means is none other than Devadatta. Great Brahmin!
If someone were to say: "
"It is said that Devadatta accumulated the karma for the hells;
one should know that this is, in fact, the karma of a bodhisattva!

The karma of a bodhisattva is precisely spiritual power (*abhijñā*); for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he appears in the hells, yet one should know that in reality he does not dwell in the hells."
For example, suppose two people travel together along a road and later go their separate ways, one to the east and one to the west.
It would be impossible to say that these people remain in union;
yet it would likewise be impossible to say that the Tathāgata and Devadatta are separated from one another.
“Great Brahmin! There are those who take life and commit evil karma; by the nature of things, they should undergo the fruits of this in hell for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
There are those who cultivate goodness; by the nature of things, they should receive the retribution for this in the heavens for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.”
There are those who cultivate goodness yet receive retribution in hell;
there are those who commit evil yet receive reward in the heavens.
This is the realm of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
The Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable, subtle, and true merits; how then can it be said that Devadatta was able to harm the Buddha’s body?
In truth, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, Devadatta gave rise to a mind of malice and rebellion toward the Tathāgata, yet he truly had no intent to cause physical harm.
Why is this? Because such a person possesses true and definitive knowledge of the retribution for good and evil.
They know that a single moment of evil leads to the reception of retribution in hell throughout immeasurable lifetimes.
For this reason, Devadatta ultimately did not commit evil.
Since the Tathāgata has forever severed all evils throughout immeasurable lifetimes, how could sentient beings give rise to an evil mind toward him?
If it is said,
"Devadatta is a person destined for hell," how can he share the same lineage as the Tathāgata, the Dharma King?
It is likewise impossible for beings in the hells to become members of the Tathāgata’s retinue.
If one were to say:
"Devadatta, having committed various evils throughout immeasurable lifetimes, ought to undergo retribution in the hells for immeasurable lifetimes," [it would be so].
"How can he dwell in the same place as the Tathāgata?
If he dwells in the same place as the Tathāgata, one should know that this person is not wicked.
If Devadatta were truly an evil person, how could he be in harmony with the Tathāgata?"
"Just as those two people travel in opposite directions, east and west, it is logically impossible for them to meet.
Devadatta followed the Buddha’s words; hearing 'east,' he went east, never contravening the Sage’s intent. How, then, can he be called a person destined for hell?"
If one were sent to the east but instead went westward in violation of the command, one could not be called a non-inhabitant of hell.
If it is said that "Devadatta is a person of hell," then there is no such thing as a person without evil.
Why is this so? "Earth" refers to humans;
"prison" refers to the heavens.
Those who wander between the realms of humans and devas are called hell-beings.
Furthermore,
"earth" (dhi) means permanence.
The name of the hell is "Signless" (Animitta); since Devadatta is also eternally signless, it is therefore named a hell.
Furthermore, "earth" (bhūmi) is called "bliss" (sukha).
"Prison" (yù) means "severance";
because one delights in severing birth and death, it is called hell (dìyù).
Furthermore!
"Earth" is a name for skillful means;
"prison" is a name for being able to teach skillful means. Therefore, it is called a hell. "Great Brahmin!"

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses skillful means and is further able to proclaim that [Devadatta] is not called a denizen of hell; how then can Devadatta be designated as a person of hell?
The realm of Devadatta is truly not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Great Brāhmaṇa! The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has always praised the "Great Being of Yellow Hair," who is none other than the Bhikṣu Devadatta.
The group of six bhikṣus were also great bodhisattvas who practiced together with Devadatta; how then could they be called denizens of hell?
They are like sandalwood trees surrounded by sandalwood;
just as when a fragrant elephant tramples, it is not something a donkey can endure, but rather something only a fragrant elephant can withstand.
"Great Brahmin! It is the same with the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Great Fragrant Elephant King.
The profound meanings he expounds cannot be understood by those of the Two Vehicles; rather, it is only the great Bodhisattvas, the Fragrant Elephants, who are able to receive and uphold them."
Devadatta has accomplished such immeasurable merits; you should repent before him, revere, make offerings to, respect, and praise him.

"Great Brahmin! If a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā is able to know the merits of Devadatta with complete clarity and without doubt, you should know that such a person is a true disciple of the Buddha; they have obtained one-half of the Buddha’s merits, one eye of the Buddha, and one half of the Buddha’s body."
"Great Brahmin! All the merits possessed by Devadatta cannot be known by any sentient beings;
likewise, all the realms of the Tathāgata’s merits cannot be known by any sentient beings, nor can they see the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata."
"Great Brahmin! Devadatta truly knows all the subtle and wondrous merits possessed by the Tathāgata, which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas truly do not know."

Only Devadatta understood this clearly without doubt; he was also able to manifest the immeasurable supernatural powers manifested by the Tathāgata, could demonstrate to sentient beings the conduct of the Tathāgata, and knew all the buddha-fields of the Buddha-Tathāgata.
Devadatta was a great man; wherever the Tathāgata traveled, Devadatta followed him everywhere.
For this reason, they are called Great Beings (Mahāpuruṣa).
The realm of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is profoundly deep; their secret words are inconceivable!
"Only the bhikṣu Devadatta is able to fully understand it.
The Tathāgata shall now reveal this secret teaching; you, sirs, should listen well!
