At that time, the great assembly, with one voice and in unison, offered this eulogy:
"Even if Māra Pāpīyas were to appear in measureless numbers,
and were to exhaust all his supernatural powers, he could not destroy the Sangha.
Such is the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed Honored One!"
"With a heart of great compassion and pity, for the sake of all sentient beings, you have manifested the retribution of karmic results.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Secret Treasury, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"You have now spoken well of the true merits of Devadatta; all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others are unable to comprehend the power and merit of the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras."
"You are about to destroy all the doubts held by all sentient beings; for this reason, you reveal and manifest the merits of the Bodhisattva Devadatta.
Furthermore, good son!"

Furthermore, this sutra contains the profound and advanced Samādhi of the Ocean Tide of All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. If there is a bodhisattva who achieves and fully possesses this samādhi, they can take Sumeru, the King of Mountains—so high, vast, firm, and solid—and blow upon it with their mouth until it is shattered like fine dust, entering into a mustard seed without the mustard seed increasing in size.

The Four Great Heavenly Kings were likewise neither startled nor terrified; they remained unbroken and unimpaired, unaware even of their own state, and the same was true for those dwelling in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment and fulfillment of the Samādhi of the Deeply Advancing Tide of the Great Ocean. Furthermore, good son!”

If there is a bodhisattva who accomplishes and fully possesses this samādhi, they may cause the waters of the four great oceans to enter a single pore without disturbing the soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, tortoises, dragons, fish, turtles, and other aquatic creatures; their lifespans remain as usual, with no loss or premature death.
The various dragon kings, asuras, and gandharvas do not even perceive where they have gone.

He is able to take the trichiliocosm and place it upon his right palm; he can sever the great earth and, like a potter’s wheel, cast it beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, yet the sentient beings therein have no perception at all of coming or going.
Taking that world and placing it back in this land is likewise so.
At that time, Śubhavyūha made offerings to the Buddha with various perfumes, flowers, banners, canopies, and music; joining his palms in reverent salutation, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you possess great compassion and cherish all beings as you do Rāhula. I now wish to make a request; I only pray that you will grant me your permission."
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer.
Then, among the assembly, there was a Licchavi youth named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, who said to Śubhavyūha:
"The Tathāgata remains silent; he has not granted his permission."
"I shall now answer you according to the questions posed by your doubts. The brāhmaṇa said, "Licchavi!"
I once heard this teaching from him:
"If one can make an offering to the Tathāgata’s relics even as small as a mustard seed, the karmic reward shall be that of the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."

“Licchavis! This *Mahāmegha Sūtra* is of profound meaning; it is the secret language of the Tathāgata, difficult to understand, and is not within the knowledge of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, let alone for people like us from the borderlands.”

"I now wish to obtain a portion of the Tathāgata’s relics, even as small as a mustard seed, to pay them respectful homage; I hope thereby to dwell in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and become the lord of that realm.
From the past until now, I have constantly held this aspiration."
At that time, the Licchavi spoke in verse:
"Suppose that in the Ganges River, lotuses were to bloom amidst the swift current, and the *kukila* birds were white; only then might the *śarīra* relics be obtained."
If a tortoise were to grow hair, which could then be used to make a *saṃghāṭī* robe that can melt ice on a winter's day, then one might obtain a *śarīra* relic;
if the legs of a mosquito were capable of serving as a bridge, [then one might obtain a *śarīra* relic].
If one could ferry across all sentient beings, then śarīra relics might be obtained;
even if leeches in the water were suddenly to grow white teeth as large as the tusks of a sandalwood elephant, then śarīra relics might be obtained.
Even if a rabbit were to grow horns, capable of serving as a ladder reaching as high as the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, then perhaps the śarīra could be obtained;
even if mice, insects, and the like were to climb that rabbit-horn ladder, [the śarīra would still not be found].
If one could ascend and eat the moon, then the *śarīra* relics might be obtained;
if even a fly could drink from a *zhong* or a *shi* of fine, pure wine,
and become so lost in delusion and addicted to intoxication that it might do so, then the *śarīra* relics might be obtained.
Even if a donkey’s lips were shaped like a *bimba* fruit,
and it were skilled in singing and dancing, only then might the *śarīra* be obtained;
even if a crow and an owl were to perch together upon the same tree, [only then might the *śarīra* be obtained].
If food and drink were never separated [from the body], then the śarīra could be obtained;
even if thorn leaves were to completely cover the entire trichiliocosm, the śarīra could be obtained.
Even if a small boat were able to carry Mount Sumeru across the great ocean, then the śarīra might be obtained;
even if a small bird were to take up the Great Fragrant Mountain in its beak—
"If it is moved elsewhere, then the *śarīra* may be obtained.
At that time, the Brahmin spoke a verse in response to the Licchavis, saying: "Excellent!"
O son of the Licchavi clan!
You are able to understand profound skillful means; now listen with a sincere mind as I speak of the Buddha’s merits.
The realm of the Buddha is inconceivable, and that which has been attained is ultimate.
The Buddhas are eternally unchanging, and therefore have no place of birth;
the physical forms of the Buddhas are equal, and this is called the Dharma-realm of the Buddhas;
the Tathāgata is not a conditioned phenomenon, nor is he one who undergoes birth.
The Tathāgata’s adamantine body cannot be destroyed;
for this reason, true śarīra cannot be found.
The Tathāgata has no śarīra, not even so much as a mustard seed.
There is no blood, flesh, or bone; how then could there be śarīra?
For the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata manifests a body of skillful means;
the bodies of all Buddhas are eternally abiding, and the Dharma-realm is likewise so.
According to the needs of all sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma through skillful means;
likewise, according to what is appropriate for each, he manifests various forms.
If the Buddha possesses compassion, it extends universally to all sentient beings.
"Why do you not manifest a division of your body to bestow śarīra relics?

At that time, there was a goddess among the assembly named Pure Light (Vimalaprabhā). She again made offerings to the Buddha with incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and music; then, with palms joined in reverence, she addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
These two sages have accomplished profound and subtle wisdom and are able to open the secret treasury of the Tathāgata; from where have they come?
We pray that you will explain this for us!
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, O goddess!”
For the sake of sentient beings, you have asked about this meaning; listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall explain it to you.
Such two persons as these are the true sons of the Buddha.
Like a king of fragrant elephants, he is a true mahāsattva.
For the sake of sentient beings, he delights in dwelling within birth and death;
knowing gratitude and repaying kindness, he is one whom I protect and keep in mind.
They are well able to protect and uphold the lineage of all Buddhas, acting as the heavy responsibility for the Buddhas by blazing brightly the lamp of the Dharma. "O Goddess!

In the past, immeasurable hundreds of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Samānagotra-pradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

At that time, there were many sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, immeasurable, boundless, and beyond calculation, all of whom attained peace, security, and happiness, free from the afflictions of hunger, thirst, suffering, and distress.

That land is vast and expansive, pure and magnificently adorned, measuring sixty-eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It contains seventy-eight thousand cities, each great city being constructed from the seven precious jewels; the four walls of each city are equipped with ninety thousand defensive towers.
"At that time, there was a great city named Ratnasaṃcaya, which is the present-day city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, there were eighty quadrillion people in the city of Ratnasaṃcaya. The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara was born in that city; all the immeasurable sentient beings therein resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attained supernatural powers, becoming elephant-kings among men."
“O Goddess! At that time, the Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, let out a lion’s roar and proclaimed this Great Cloud Sūtra.
At that time, in that city, there was a king named Dragon King Mahāvīrya; the king had a queen named Dharmapālā, and he had a chief minister named Dharma-vana-koṭi.”

At that time, the king, together with his queen and his ministers, went to where the Buddha was; having made offerings and paid him respect, they joined their palms in salutation, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata Samānajāti-pradīpa, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Dragon King Mahāvīrya, emitted a great radiance named Fearlessness.
When the King encountered this light, his heart attained the joy of the Dharma.
At that time, the great minister, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Can the relics of the Tathāgata be obtained?”
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer. "O Goddess!
At that time, for the sake of the True Dharma, the Great King, together with his ministers, repeatedly deliberated and discussed the śarīra."
When the Buddha heard this, he immediately praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Within that assembly of the Buddha, there was a great disciple named Mahānāman, who conceived a virtuous aspiration and thought to himself:
"Excellent, Great King! You have well understood the profound Dharma-realm of the Tathāgata."

At that time, the Buddha immediately expounded for the great assembly gathered there the profound Dharma and subtle meanings understood by the King; having heard this, the entire assembly was filled with wonder and doubt.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"The merit of this king is inconceivable and its depth unfathomable; it is not something you are capable of understanding."

At that time, when the Great King heard the Buddha praise his own merit, his heart was filled with great joy. He immediately rose to make offerings, circumambulating the Buddha a thousand times to the right. Taking jewel-like flowers he had gathered, he scattered them over the Buddha and further offered praise, then made this vow:

"In the future, when the Tathāgata Śākyamuni appears in the world and, through great skillful means, demonstrates the time of the Dharma’s extinction, I shall renounce the household life therein to cultivate the Way, uphold the pure precepts, and possess great power."
If I see bhikṣus who have broken the precepts and practice evil, I shall expel them to remote regions where the Buddha-dharma does not exist.
For the sake of the True Dharma, I will not spare even my own body or life.
At that time, the great minister further made this vow:
"Once Śākyamuni Tathāgata has manifested his parinirvāṇa through great skillful means, I shall become a great king therein and protect and uphold the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed True Dharma."
"Upon seeing wicked bhikṣus, I shall proclaim their faults and drive them out;
toward those who uphold the Dharma, I shall pay respect and provide offerings.
At that time, the lady again made this vow:
"When Śākyamuni Tathāgata appears in the world, may my power enable me to subdue those with false views.
Then, Mahānāman made this further vow:
"May I, at that time, become a great disciple of that Tathāgata, attain great supernormal powers, and be able to roar the lion's roar regarding the Buddha’s merits."
“O Goddess! These four persons are now the ones entrusted with the heavy responsibility for the Dharma in my world.
Not only today, but in the future as well, they shall further protect and uphold my True Dharma.”
At that time, the goddess addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not yet know who these four persons are. I only pray that the Tathāgata will tell me their names.”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, goddess! Listen attentively and listen attentively with a sincere heart!"
"I shall now analyze and explain this for you.
At that time, the great minister was none other than the present Brahmin Śrīmitra.

After my parinirvāṇa, two hundred years hence, this Brahmin will become king of Jambudvīpa; his name will be Aśoka, he will reside in the city of Pāṭaliputra, his clan name will be Vatsa, and he will possess one-half of all the merit of a Cakravartin King, attaining great sovereignty over Jambudvīpa."

They uphold the true Dharma, let out the great lion’s roar, and cause the Dharma to circulate widely; they obtain great quantities of relics, which they honor, revere, respect, and praise; and upon seeing wicked bhikṣus, they discipline them so that they may cultivate goodness.
The goddess spoke again:
"I pray that you will explain this.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the goddess:
“Wait but a moment; I shall first explain your own causal conditions.
When the goddess heard these words, she immediately felt shame and remorse, lowering her head and prostrating herself upon the ground.
The Buddha then praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Indeed, a sense of shame and remorse is the garment of wholesome dharmas for sentient beings."
"O Goddess! The queen of that king at that time was none other than your own self.

Because you briefly heard the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* from that Buddha, by this causal condition, you have now obtained a celestial body; having encountered my appearance in the world, you have again heard its profound meaning. You shall cast off this celestial form and, in the very body of a woman, rule over a kingdom, obtaining a quarter of the territory governed by a Wheel-Turning King."

Having attained great mastery, she received and upheld the five precepts and became an upāsikā, teaching and transforming the men and women, both young and old, within her affiliated cities and villages.
You upheld the five precepts, guarded the True Dharma, and subdued the various heterodox views of the non-Buddhists.
At that time, you were truly a Bodhisattva who manifested in a female body for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
The king at that time was none other than the present Li-chi (Likhita), whom all sentient beings delight to behold.

He has profoundly penetrated the most profound meaning of the True Dharma, is able to open the subtle and secret Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata, and protects and upholds the Buddha-dharma without any impairment.

At that time, Mahānāman was none other than the present Bodhisattva Mahāmeghagambhīrakośa; he has attained one-half of my true body, recognizes kindness and repays it, protects and upholds the True Dharma, and is able to answer profound meanings without any obstruction.
"O Goddess!

Although this assembly of mine includes those of superior wisdom such as Mahākāśyapa, they are unable to expound and debate the profoundly deep meaning in the manner of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Cloud Secret Treasury."

At that time, there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Extraordinary Talent (*Viśeṣacintin*), who, together with a thousand sons of heaven, immediately rose and approached the Buddha. He made offerings to the Buddha with various flowers, incense, banners, canopies, and music; joining his palms in reverence, he praised the Buddha in verse:
"The great ocean may be measured, And Mount Sumeru may be weighed and known, But the realm of the Tathāgata’s Dharma Is difficult to conceive or imagine!"
When this Dharma was being taught, countless thousands of people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed Śubhavyūha, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Great Brahmin! You have now well aroused a heart of joy and shall attain the unsurpassed fruit. Great Brahmin!"

From here, traveling southward across worlds as numerous as the sands of three hundred thousand Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sumanā. Therein dwells a Buddha, a World-Honored One, titled Pure Light Secret Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He constantly abides in the world, transforming sentient beings and turning the wheel of the True Dharma.

From there, proceeding southward and crossing further fifty hundred thousand worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a world named Jewel of Dharma-Joy. Therein dwells a Buddha named Dharmagarbha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; he constantly remains in the world, transforming sentient beings and turning the wheel of the sublime Dharma.

Going south from there, passing again through worlds as numerous as the sands of six hundred thousand Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sarvapuṣkariṇī. There, the Buddha is named Siṃhanāda-Ṛddhirāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He dwells permanently in the world, transforming sentient beings and turning the wheel of the sublime Dharma.

Traveling south from there, passing again through as many worlds as there are grains of sand in three million sixty thousand Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Flower Banner (*Puṣpadhvaja*). Therein dwells a Buddha named High Sumeru (*Sumerupravṛddha*), who is endowed with the ten titles and even turns the wheel of the sublime Dharma.

Going south from there, passing again through worlds as numerous as the sands of eight hundred thousand Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Ratnapāṇi; the Buddha there is named Dharmarakṣa, who is endowed with the ten titles, and so forth, up to his turning of the wheel of the sublime Dharma.
"Great Brahmin! Such are the Buddha-worlds: their lands are adorned and purified, being free from mountains, hills, mounds, stones, sand, and any impurities."
The ground there is soft and supple, like kāliṅga cloth.

There are no five corruptions in that world; nor are there female bodies or those of the two vehicles, nor even the names of the two vehicles or the word "woman. It is composed entirely of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who delight in the Mahāyāna, protect and uphold the Mahāyāna, and joyfully expound the Mahāyāna.
"Great Brahmin! If there should be any son or daughter of good family who upholds the names of these Buddhas and yet falls into the three evil paths, such a thing is impossible;
they will certainly and surely attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Great Brahmin! For this reason, after my parinirvāṇa, this sutra shall be widely circulated and propagated in the lands of the south.

When the True Dharma is about to perish, with forty years remaining, it shall reach the north. There will be a king in the north named Anle (Peace and Bliss), who, seeing those who receive, uphold, copy, read, recite, or explain this scripture, shall provide them with timely gifts and offerings so that they lack nothing in the four requisites."
At that time, there shall be eighty-four thousand sentient beings in the northern direction who will receive and uphold this sūtra volume.
Good son! If there were anyone who, having heard such a sūtra as this, would abandon, relinquish, or distance themselves from it—that is impossible.

If there are good sons or good daughters who wear upon their heads and uphold the names of the Buddhas, it is impossible for them to encounter harm from military conflict, poison, water, fire, or bandits, except as a result of their past karma.
Furthermore, Great Brahmin!

Whether they be members of the fourfold assembly within or sentient beings without, if for the sake of making offerings, out of fear, or even for the sake of destroying the Dharma, they uphold the names of these Buddhas, they shall never fall into the three evil realms; it is impossible that they should reach those three evil realms.
At that time, Śubhavyūha spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
If sentient beings who merely hear the name of this sutra obtain such immeasurable and virtuous benefits, how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or explain it?”

If one is able to hear the names of those Buddhas, it means one has already obtained the unsurpassed great treasure; Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is already in one's hand, and the Tathāgatas have already arrived at one's dwelling.
Their ground is adamantine, and their bodies are likewise; their minds are firm and unmoving, incapable of being shifted or turned.
World-Honored One!
I shall now also reverently make offerings to such persons as these.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Great Brahmin!"
You now well know and well understand the power of the Tathāgata’s merits.

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the name of that Buddha, revere and believe it without doubt, they shall be free from all fears—namely, fear of kings, fear of men, and fear of ghosts—and shall be free from all diseases.
"He shall always be protected by the disciples of the Buddhas who study the Path, by the eight classes of spirits and their retinues, and he shall be held in the mindful remembrance of all Buddhas.
At that time, there was among the assembly a Gandharva King named Priyadarśana, who rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, what kind of sentient beings will be able to receive, uphold, and widely disseminate this sutra?
And what kind of sentient beings will be unable to receive and uphold it, thereby causing the Dharma to perish?
At that time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not answer.
Then, Mahākāśyapa said to Priyadarśana, “Good son!...”
The Tathāgata is truly without nirvāṇa, and dharmas are without extinction; why then do you say:
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, who shall receive this sutra?"
King Priyadarśana said: "O Virtuous One!
All sentient beings are deluded, ignorant, and devoid of wisdom; I only pray that the Virtuous One will proclaim why the Tathāgata does not pass into extinction."
All sentient beings are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance; I vow to light the lamp of Dharma so that they may attain illumination.
In the future, I shall also extensively expound this meaning for the sake of all sentient beings.
"I only pray that the Venerable One will speak out of compassion! Mahākāśyapa replied,
"Son of good family!
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not called a physical body.

The Buddha’s body is adamantine; it is not a destructible body, but a body that has fully accomplished immeasurable merit and skillful means. It is not called a body sustained by food. How can such a body be said to perish?
King Priyadarśana said, "Virtuous One!
I now know for certain that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa through skillful means; it is not an ultimate extinction."
At that time, Kāśyapa praised Sudarśana, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is truly as you have said."
"Good son! The great ocean may be measured, but the merit of the Tathāgata cannot be fully known.
King Priyadarśana said:
"When will the Tathāgata finally enter parinirvāṇa?
Mahākāśyapa replied, "If all sentient beings,
even down to the mosquitoes and ants, were to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and enter nirvāṇa, only then would the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa."
King Priyadarśana said: "Virtuous One!
Since the Tathāgata has accomplished such immeasurable and boundless merits, for what reason do all sentient beings not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Alas, alas! Sentient beings have meager merit;
they do not know that the Tathāgata possesses an eternally abiding, unchanging, adamantine body, and not a body sustained by various foods.
O Virtuous One!
"A body such as this can only be known by a Buddha; it is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Kāśyapa spoke again: "Good son!..."
"All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature and shall attain the bodhicitta.
When this Dharma was being taught, twenty-two thousand devaputras resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and with one voice and in unison, they spoke these verses:
"The Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa; The true Dharma never ceases to exist."
For the sake of all sentient beings, he manifests the appearance of passing into extinction;
yet the Tathāgata is eternally non-extinct, teaching through various skillful means for the sake of the multitude.
The Tathāgata is inconceivable, and so too are the Dharma and the Saṅgha!
The Mahāvaipulya Amogha-samādhi Sūtra, Scroll Four;
The Mahāvaipulya Amogha-samādhi Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
37. The First Part of the Vṛddhivardhana-khaṇḍa, the Great Cloud Sūtra: Vṛddhivardhana-khaṇḍa Thirty-Seven, Part One.

At that time, there were immeasurable numbers of devaputras from the south who came from the Black Mountains to where the Buddha was. They made offerings to the Buddha with various incenses, flowers, banners, canopies, and music; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

As the Tathāgata preaches this sutra today, so too do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in worlds as immeasurable and boundless as the sands of the Ganges in the southern direction, preach this very sutra.
“World-Honored One!
What is the name of such a sutra as this? “Good son!”
This sutra has three titles: first, "The Great Cloud"; second, "The Great Parinirvāṇa"; and third, "The Non-conceptual."
It is called "Great Cloud" because it was requested by the Bodhisattva Mahāmegha-garbha;
it is called "Mahāparinirvāṇa" because the Tathāgata abides eternally and there is no one who enters ultimate nirvana, for all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
and it is called "Non-conceptual" because by upholding, receiving, reading, and reciting such a sutra as this, one severs all conceptualizations.

“Good son! There are those who have drawn near to Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers; under those Buddhas, they have upheld the pure precepts, made offerings, shown reverence, and offered praise, thereby accomplishing great merit, and only then are they able to hear this sutra.
Although they have heard and received it, they are unable to explain it extensively.”

If one has upheld the pure precepts under incalculable and innumerable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and has even accomplished great merit, then upon hearing [this teaching], one will be able to discern and explain it in detail.
“Good son! When the True Dharma is about to perish, this sutra shall be fully disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa;
it shall likewise be disseminated during the first forty years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.”
When the True Dharma is on the verge of extinction with only forty years remaining, it shall once again be disseminated.
At a time when evil is practiced, when the Vaipulya sutras are slandered, when wicked kings rule, and when my disciples violate the prohibitions and precepts; [it shall be disseminated].
When encountering the chaos of a time of ruin, the people of the world treat the age with contempt;

when the disciples of the fourfold assembly do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate precepts, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom; when they are maddened by ignorance and delusion, practicing heedlessness;
and when all their actions are no different from those of beasts.
When they do not follow the instructions of their preceptors and teachers;
when they oppose the elders, the seniors, and the venerable ones— at such times,
my disciples will be unable to believe and accept this sutra, but will instead mock it with derision and censure, mutually disparaging one another.
"How can false views be called Vaipulya?
One who has shaved his head is called a śramaṇa; why then do you read scriptures of false views in reverse?
These are not truly the words of the Buddha, yet for the sake of gain and support, you claim they are the words of the Buddha."
In the midst of the assembly, the official proclaimed these words:
"A sutra such as this is truly a teaching of false views; it was not spoken by the Buddha. Be careful not to read, recite, transcribe, or uphold it."
At that time, the great assembly replied together, saying:
"Virtuous One! Do not speak such words. The characteristics and meaning of this sutra are truly taught by the Buddha; we shall now provide you with whatever you require for the sake of the sutra."
"This disciple of mine, for the sake of making offerings, accepts, upholds, recites, and explains [the teachings] without having any prior faith; this is called 'the destruction of the Dharma.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!"

In future ages, when the Dharma is about to perish, my fourfold assembly will have meager merit and little wisdom; they will not know contentment, will fall away from their roots of goodness, and will be impoverished of the wealth of the Dharma.

They have no sincere devotion to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; they shave their heads and dye their robes merely for the sake of food and clothing. Their minds are coarse and unruly, like those of shaven-headed laymen who keep slaves and servants, gold, silver, precious jewels, money, cowries, lapis lazuli, and crystal; they hoard grain and rice, cattle, horses, livestock, fields, lands, and houses.
Using variegated bedding and sitting mats, eating meat and indulging in savory flavors, they turn their backs on all Buddhas and accomplish sixteen unwholesome codes of discipline.
They associate with kings, ministers, and elders, acting as envoys to neighboring states to convey messages and decrees.
"Receiving offerings from others, they instead give rise to evil thoughts.
They accomplish all that is contrary to the dharma of śramaṇas and contrary to the dharma of brāhmaṇas. O Devaputra!"

In such an evil age, during the time of wicked bhikṣus, I shall then have a disciple who maintains pure precepts, has few desires and is contented, like Mahākāśyapa, and who is well able to transform those among my disciples within Jambudvīpa who practice evil.

He speaks words of truth, disregarding even his own body and life; he extensively reveals the profound and secret treasury of the Tathāgata, praises those who uphold the precepts and practice the dhūta austerities, and is fully accomplished in the prātimokṣa.
Praising contentment and wearing robes made of discarded rags, he spoke these words at length to wicked people:
"Venerable sirs! The World-Honored One does not permit the acceptance or possession of any impure things, nor does He allow the greedy consumption of meat."
The Tathāgata always praises those who maintain pure precepts and rebukes those who violate the prohibitions.
Venerable One!
If you do not now accept my words, I possess great power and might, and am able to subdue you.
"By the power of the merit of this disciple of mine, I cause all beings to believe and submit without opposition. Why is this?

Because this person has already drawn near to immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, extensively cultivated loving-kindness and compassion, delighted in the Mahāyāna, and protected the True Dharma."
“At that time, there were always fifty-eight thousand benevolent spirits and deities who followed and attended upon him, desiring to protect the Buddha’s true Dharma.
The devaputra spoke again:
“World-Honored One!”
"We, too, shall protect these bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma in the future.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Son of Heaven!
It is as you have said: when the Dharma is about to perish, one must diligently protect it.
O Son of Heaven!"
At that time, I shall also be able to subdue evil Māras and discipline wicked bhikṣus through my majestic spiritual power.
At that moment, the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions will likewise join in praising this disciple of mine.
At that time, all the devaputras from the southern direction again made offerings of flowers and incense to the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When will such disciples emerge?"
"In which land does he dwell,
and what is his name?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! One thousand two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a great king in the land of South India named Śatavāhana.”

When the Dharma is on the verge of extinction, with only forty years remaining, this person shall appear at that time to preach and proclaim the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras. They shall rescue and restore the Dharma that is about to perish, causing this scripture to spread widely throughout the world, and instructing people to fully uphold, recite, transcribe, explain, and listen to its meaning.

At that time, if there are those who are unable to receive, uphold, explain, and expound this sutra in this manner, you should know that such persons are not my disciples, but are the retinue of Māra.
At that time, the Gandharva King Priyadarśana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I pray that you will compassionately explain this for me: how may future disciples who uphold the Dharma, such as Kāśyapa, achieve great loving-kindness, be fully endowed with pure precepts, and possess a lineage and retinue beyond reproach?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall explain this for you.
This disciple of mine protects the True Dharma, upholds the lineage of the Buddhas, and is one whom all sentient beings delight to behold.
O son of good family!
In South India, there was a small kingdom named Sūrata; in that land there was a river named Suparikarman, and along that river there was a village named Puṣpamāla.

In the village of Mālyagrāma, there was a brāhmaṇa who gave birth to a boy; he is none other than the Licchavi Sarvadarśanīya of today. Later, he was also named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana. He is a great bodhisattva, a great fragrant elephant king, who is constantly honored, supported, revered, and praised by all.

At the age of twenty, he left the household life to practice the Way; he gathered many disciples and maintained the pure precepts, chanting the Mahāyāna sūtras of the Buddhas and sacrificing his own body and life to protect the True Dharma.
His disciples likewise did so.
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who hear this true Dharma spoken by this bhikṣu, they will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the kings, ministers, elders, and all people, for the sake of this sutra, shall offer worship and respect to those who uphold the Dharma; by the power of this sutra, they shall cause those kings to attain great authority, such that no one will be able to invade or oppress their lands.
"Regarding this disciple of mine, Māra shall find no opportunity.

At that time, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, or transcribe this sutra, they shall be called great bodhisattvas; they shall be called fields of merit, and they shall be reckoned among the pure saṃgha.
Gandharva King! At that time, many of my disciples will have faith in and accept such sutras as these, and those who attain liberation will likewise not be few.
"Good son! If there is anyone who can accomplish four matters, they will be able to receive and uphold such a sutra as this:
first, they shall attain the profound and advancing ocean-tide samādhi;..."
Second, hearing the names of the Buddhas of the southern quarter;
third, drawing near to spiritual friends;
fourth, believing with a sincere heart in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
At that time, those who are unable to believe and accept this sutra are the retinue of Māra;
those who do believe are the disciples of the Buddha. Good son!
In future ages, those who possess faith shall be called "those who draw near to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Why is this? Such sutras as these are the seals of all Buddhas.
As for what is called the "seal": all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature; the Tathāgata is eternally present and undergoes no change or transformation.
Good son! If there is anyone who can believe in this sutra, you should know that such a person is a true disciple of the Buddha.
Whoever is able to show reverence to such a holder of the Dharma will become a member of the retinue and followers of all future Buddhas.
Why is this? Because immeasurable Buddhas have already given rise to the thought of treating that person as their own child.
Why is this? This Dharma-holding bhikṣu is inconceivable; in the past, he made a great vow together with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, saying:

"In a future age, when the Dharma of Śākyamuni Tathāgata is on the verge of extinction, I shall go forth from home to practice the Way therein, and for the sake of protecting the True Dharma, I will not spare my own body or life."
"The King named Vigorous Dragon at that time was none other than the Licchavi Sunetra of the present day.
This Licchavi Sunetra is himself the bhikṣu who will protect the Dharma in the future."
“Good son! You have skillfully observed the future merits of this disciple of mine.

If there is anyone who can respectfully make offerings to this disciple of mine, you should know that such a person will be respected by all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.”

If, in future ages, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās place their faith in and accept what is thus expounded by a bhikṣu who upholds the Dharma, they are thereby placing their faith in and accepting all the words spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions.

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who love and revere such Dharma-holding bhikṣus, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives, they will be cherished and remembered by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and their lifespans will increase.

If, in future ages, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās should respectfully make offerings to these upholders of the Dharma, focusing their minds with single-minded mindfulness, listening to what they preach without seeking out their faults, they shall be sought after and protected by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, who will guard and maintain them just as Rāhula was protected and mindful of the prohibitive precepts.
“Good son! In future ages, sentient beings of meager merit—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—will speak thus: ‘Alas, alas!’”
Such sentient beings delight in seeing bhikṣus who are not truly bhikṣus but merely assume the appearance of bhikṣus.
They distance themselves from the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas and instead proclaim their own compositions, calling them the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*;
they distance themselves from the prohibitions and precepts established by the Buddhas and instead establish their own prohibitions and precepts for the sake of sentient beings.
Venerable sirs!
Each of you listen attentively!
If one says that storing gold, silver, and precious treasures is called breaking the precepts, while not storing them is called upholding the precepts.
"In what place did the Tathāgata ever speak such words?
This is not the Buddha’s teaching, yet you claim it is the Buddha’s teaching.

How could I, at the cost of my own body and life, pay respect and make offerings to such evil people who proclaim wicked speech as the Buddha’s word and chant out evil precepts as the Buddha’s precepts?"
"Venerable sirs!
I truly cannot believe or accept the words of such evil bhikṣus.
If anyone makes offerings to such persons as these, their merit will be wasted in vain, and they shall ultimately receive no karmic fruit."
At that time, having heard these words, all their faith was individually destroyed and extinguished.
If there were those who believed and accepted these evil words, you should know that such people go from darkness into darkness;
if they do not believe and accept them, such people will instead go from light into light.
“Good son! If there are those who comply with such evil speech, they are the retinue of Māra;
if they do not comply, they are truly my disciples.”
"Good son! This *Mahāmegha Sūtra* is profound and subtle in its meaning, difficult to comprehend.
If, in a future age, there are members of the fourfold assembly whose merit is pure and thick, who have attained the bodhicitta and diligently practice, they will speak thus:"
“Excellent, bhikṣu! You are a true disciple of the Buddha!”
Firmly established upon the great earth, this is a Mahāsattva;
a valiant Great Being, not an inferior person.
An inferior person could not turn back the great ocean in such a manner.
Venerable sirs!
You should come; we shall together make offerings to such a bhikṣu.
Venerable sirs!
I now see that this bhikṣu who upholds the Dharma is the fruit of immeasurable merit from past lives.
Wherever this bhikṣu dwells, you should know that the land and its sentient beings will have their merit fully perfected, and they shall dwell in peace, happiness, and freedom from affliction.
If one should behold such a bhikṣu, it should be known that this person has already attained the divine eye and is fully endowed with the Dharma-eye.
For the sake of such a person, I would not spare my own body or life;
if I hear their words, I would rather sacrifice my body and life than ever forget them.

I would rather, for the sake of such a single person, not spare my own body or life; I could never, for the sake of hundreds of thousands of millions of people who are partisans of unrighteousness, sacrifice my body or life.
"Good son! When such evil dharmas arise, this disciple of mine shall, amidst them, protect and uphold my Dharma."

“Good son! In future ages, when the Dharma is about to perish, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, do not begrudge their own bodies or lives, these are called those who kindle the lamp of wisdom to deliver and liberate sentient beings.”
Practicing all that is practiced by the Buddhas, they attain the wings of the Dharma and shatter the realms of Māra.
They achieve mastery over the body and mastery over the mind; their bodies are inconceivable, and they are beloved and revered by all sentient beings.
“Good son! When the Dharma is about to perish, those who uphold the Dharma shall, for one day and one night, chant and proclaim at six intervals, announcing to all sentient beings:
‘You all should together receive and uphold the True Dharma.’”
When the wicked bhikṣus heard these words, their hearts were not pleased; because they were not pleased, they spoke thus:
"Venerable One!..."
Who would ever believe and accept such false teachings?
It would be well for you to remain silent;
if you do not remain silent, we shall take your life.
This upholder of the Dharma further said:
"I would rather give up my life than remain silent.
Thereupon, the wicked bhikṣus collectively harmed this bhikṣu who upheld the Dharma.
“Good son! Such a person as this is my final disciple who upholds the Dharma.
You should know that at that time, my Dharma will then perish.”
"If one were to say that at that time there would be anyone else among my disciples who could likewise protect and uphold the Dharma, such a thing is impossible.
The Gandharva King asked:
"After this upholder of the Dharma has cast off this body, what kind of body will he obtain?"
The Buddha said,
"Good son! Having cast off this body, you shall attain the body of a Buddha, a boundless body."
The Gandharva King said:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for the sake of all sentient beings, explain how this bhikṣu abandons his body and attains the body of a Buddha."
The Buddha said:
"Good son! Excellent, excellent!"
Listen as I speak of the merits of this disciple who upholds the Dharma.
After these Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa have passed into extinction, for a full sixty-two thousand kalpas, time shall pass in vain without a Buddha appearing.
At that time, there will be immeasurable billions of nayutas of pratyekabuddhas who will dwell in the world teaching and transforming beings.
After this kalpa has passed, seven buddhas will appear.
After these seven Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa, this land shall then be renamed Joyful Light (Prabhāsa).

In that land of Joyful Light, a Buddha shall appear, known as Jñānaskandhaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
In that Buddha-world, all the people will have upright and handsome features and be perfected in faith.
If there are those who can protect and uphold my Dharma until the end of their lives, they shall all be born in that Buddha-world and become great disciples of that Buddha.
The great disciples are none other than the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—true great men and great fragrant elephant kings.
The people of that realm are entirely free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and have all fully accomplished pure faith.
“The Buddha Jñānarāśiprabha lived for fifteen intermediate kalpas and, for the sake of his disciples, expounded the teachings of the three vehicles.
Although he established the three vehicles, he primarily taught the practice of the single vehicle of the bodhisattvas.”
At that time, although there were Māras and sons of Māras, they all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
all sentient beings attained the mind of great kindness and great compassion, and all were able to remain far removed from the sufferings of the three evil realms, free from the eight difficulties.
The world is eternally pure, just like the northern continent of Uttarakuru.
The celestial Māra Pāpīyān finds no opportunity there, and false views are forever severed.
After that Buddha-Tathāgata enters nirvana, the Dharma shall remain for a thousand koṭis of years, and only thereafter will it be completely extinguished.

When these words were spoken, the entire great assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—made offerings to the Buddha with various flowers, incense, and exquisite music.
Mahākāśyapa and the other great disciples rejoiced and praised him, paying homage with deep reverence.
The great bodhisattvas, in turn, took wonderful flowers as large as Mount Sumeru and offered them to the Buddha, all together making this vow:
“May I, in the future, be born in the world of that Buddha!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmeghaghanagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will, for the sake of sentient beings of meager merit in future ages, expound this profound Samādhi of the Advancing Ocean Tide.
The Buddha said, “Good son!
You should not speak in such a manner now. Why is this?

The appearance of a Buddha in the world is rare; it is likewise rare to hear this *Mahāmegha Sūtra*. Furthermore, for anyone to transcribe, receive and uphold, or read and recite even a single phrase or a single word of it is also exceedingly difficult to attain.
Why do you say it is intended specifically for people of the future?
I shall universally expound and analyze this for the sake of sentient beings of the three periods of time. Good son!
Because sentient beings of future generations will have meager merit and their roots of sin will be deep and heavy, I therefore proclaim this sutra so that it shall circulate in the future. Good son!
In future ages, if there should be those who, with faith and without doubt, read or recite even a single verse from this *Mahāmegha Sūtra*, such persons will be exceedingly rare to find.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the Tathāgata speak these words? “Good son!”
I do not speak thus only for the sake of the future; why, then, have you conceived such a doubt?

If there were anyone capable of hearing even a single verse or a single line spoken by the Tathāgata without giving rise to doubt, such a person would be difficult to find throughout the three periods of time.
Why is this? Sentient beings of the three periods of time find it difficult to attain the samādhi and dhāraṇī gates that allow them to recognize kindness and repay their debts of gratitude.
Sentient beings of the future will not know how to acknowledge the measure of kindness they receive, nor will they be able to repay that kindness.
Because they do not recognize kindness, faith is difficult to obtain;
because faith is difficult to obtain, I have said:
"I preach this sutra for the sake of future generations."
"If one can read, recite, receive, and uphold even a single verse or a single phrase of this sutra, such a person is difficult to find.
Because future sentient beings will have meager merit and heavy transgressions, he further says:
"For the sake of future generations, I shall preach this scripture."
The Bodhisattva Mahāmeghaguhyagarbha said:
“World-Honored One!

If there are bodhisattvas who dwell securely in this profound and advanced Samādhi of the Ocean Tide, they will accomplish immeasurable and boundless merits, which are not within the knowledge of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!"
The bodhisattvas who dwell in this samādhi are profoundly unfathomable!
They are like the great ocean, into which all streams flow, beyond measure or calculation. Good son!
Even such a great ocean may yet be measured and numbered, but the bodhisattvas cannot be measured or numbered.
Why is this? Because they dwell securely in such profound samādhi.
"Furthermore, good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in this samādhi, he can, with a single hair on his toe, lift up these great trichiliocosm worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, raising them as high as immeasurable worlds above, so that all sentient beings therein feel no fear or thought of coming and going, yet are seen by everyone in other regions for the sake of their transformation and deliverance;
even throughout the ten directions, it is likewise so."
“World-Honored One!
This samādhi is accomplished through immeasurable and boundless merit; therefore, the Buddha has said:
‘It universally benefits all three periods of time.’”
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
It is truly as you have said!”
"Good son! Just as the great ocean encompasses all rivers and streams, so too is this *Mahāmegha Sūtra*; it likewise encompasses all immeasurable sūtras."
"Furthermore, good son!
If there are any sūtras that contain such samādhis as this 'Unattached Samādhi,' you should know that those sūtras are already subsumed within this present sūtra."
The samādhis attained by all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others cannot be compared to this samādhi; they do not even serve as a metaphor for it. Why is this?
Because for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there is no permanence, no self, no bliss, and no purity.
The samādhi of non-attachment extensively reveals the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which are without change; therefore, these two cannot be compared to one another. "Good son!

If one hears that the Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging, and their faith becomes pure, you should know that this person has attained the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and is cultivating the path to enlightenment.
"Good son! Whether male or female, those who wish to attain the eternal and unchanging state should receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, and expound this sutra."
If one can thus receive, uphold, and expound this sutra, you should know that such a person shall before long attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If there are those who, upon hearing that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change, give rise to doubt and fear, you should know that such persons do not perceive the true mark of the Tathāgata.
As for the true characteristic, it is that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging, abiding in serene stillness.
Therefore, those who hear this should not harbor doubt or fear;
they should receive and uphold it, and widely expound it for others.
Those who speak thus should know that the Buddha-dharma is eternally abiding and never extinguished. "Good son!
Just as the tracks of all sentient beings are contained within the footprint of an elephant, so too are all samādhis contained within this sutra."

"Good son! Just as all the mountains, rivers, groves, and trees of Jambudvīpa, as well as the mountains, rivers, trees, sun, moon, and constellations of the four continents, are all contained within the trichiliocosm."
The merits, meditative concentrations, and samādhis of all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas and bodhisattvas are likewise entirely contained within this *Mahāmegha Sūtra*.

If there are sentient beings who, for even a single thought-moment, can contemplate all Tathāgatas as eternally abiding and unchanging, you should know that they immediately attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Good son! It is like the autumn moon when there are no clouds or mist and the sky is pure; when the sun first rises, its radiance is majestic and beautiful, loved and cherished by all people, as it dispels all deep darkness and gloom.

This *Mahāmegha Sūtra* is likewise so: it brings forth the Tathāgata, who is eternal, constant, and unchanging—a blazing sun situated within the space of pure secret speech—to shatter the darkness of all sentient beings' ignorance regarding impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity.
"One who is dignified and lovely" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, who never ultimately enters parinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, good son! For example, there is a person whose body is light and whose movement is swift; this is a metaphor for the four wind-kings."
Their lifespan was fulfilled, lasting for many thousands of celestial years.
They traveled by flight throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and having completed their circuit, returned to their original dwelling place.
In this manner, they filled the realms of their travels with the seven treasures and, including their own bodies, made offerings to the Triple Gem for countless thousands of years.
“Good son! Can such merit be measured? “No, it cannot.”
“World-Honored One!
‘Good son, such merit cannot compare with that of someone who, in a single thought-moment, contemplates the Tathāgata as eternal and the Dharma and Saṅgha as imperishable.’”

"Good son! If there should be another person who, for the sake of gain and support, for the sake of fear, or for the sake of intimacy, expounds even a single word or a single phrase concerning the Tathāgata’s permanence, constancy, and immutability, the merit obtained by that person would not equal even one hundredth part of the former merit; it would not equal one thousandth, nor one hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor could it be reached even by calculation or analogy."
“Good son! It is like a medicinal tree: if there are sentient beings who take its branches, its trunk, its leaves, its flowers, its fruits, or its bark, this tree does not give rise to the thought:
‘Take the branches; do not take the trunk;’”
Take the stem, but do not take the leaves;
take the leaves, but do not take the flowers;
take the flowers, but do not take the fruit.
"Take the fruit; do not take the skin.
Thus, it causes all manner of illnesses to be cured, according to the needs of sentient beings of superior, middling, or inferior capacity.
Whether mixed with water, or mixed with clarified butter (sarpis), whether as powder, pills, ointment, or an internal decoction, it is capable of curing every disease.

This *Mahāmegha Sūtra* is also like this: it does not discriminate among sentient beings. Whether one recites a single verse, or half a verse, a single name, a single meaning, a single phrase, or even half a phrase; or if one merely accepts with faith the two words "the Tathāgata is eternal," or speaks of the Tathāgata as being permanent—it does not observe whether sentient beings are practicing the profound and advancing ocean-tide samādhi, great kindness, or great compassion, nor whether they are not so practicing; it is able to cause them all to sever the maladies of the three evil realms.

The Tathāgata likewise does not observe sentient beings by taking a single verse while discarding half a verse; nor by taking half a verse while discarding its name; nor by taking the name while discarding its meaning; nor by taking the meaning while discarding the phrase; nor by taking the phrase while discarding half a phrase; nor by taking half a phrase down to even two characters—yet he is able to cause the fourfold assembly to leave the three evil realms behind.

“Good son! In the future, there will be people who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate morality, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom; they will treat this [teaching] with derision, contempt, and arrogance, seeking out faults and motivated by gain and offerings. Yet, even those who read, recite, transcribe, or listen to it only a little shall be able to distance themselves from immeasurable evil karma and forever sever the maladies of greed, hatred, and delusion.”
“Good son! Just as when the sun rises it can melt ice and snow, so too is this *Mahāmegha Sūtra*:
by teaching the permanence of the Tathāgata, it can melt all the ice and snow of impermanence.”
"Furthermore, good son! It is like the empty sky:

when a fierce wind arises, it blows upon the bodies of sentient beings, entering through all their pores, able to cause every feverish ailment to be completely cured, so that the body attains coolness and clarity."
The empty space is a metaphor for the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*;
the rising of a fierce wind is a metaphor for the permanence of the Tathāgata;
and the wind entering the pores is a metaphor for the fact that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature.
"Curing fever" is a metaphor for severing the mindsets of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, good son, if there is anyone who can read,
recite, receive, and uphold such a sutra as this, they will never [aim] for the fruit of srotāpanna."
Maintaining the prohibitive precepts, one never becomes a candidate for the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin nor attains the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin;
nor a candidate for Anāgāmin nor attains the fruit of Anāgāmin;
nor a candidate for Arhat nor attains the fruit of Arhat.

To uphold the precepts for the sake of turning toward the Buddha and attaining the unsurpassed fruit is what is called truly upholding the precepts; it is not for the sake of the thirty-two marks or eighty minor characteristics that one upholds the precepts. Only when it is for the sake of the inconceivable Tathāgata is it called upholding the precepts.

The Tathāgata does not dwell the mind to cultivate and accumulate immeasurable samādhis, nor does he dwell the mind to cultivate and accumulate equality with all Buddhas, nor does he dwell the mind to cultivate and accumulate immeasurable causes and effects, nor does he dwell the mind to cultivate and accumulate the immeasurable merits of all Buddhas.
That the Tathāgata abides in non-abiding is the true mark (*dharmatā*).
If one deceives the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed seal, one cannot be said to be guarding the precepts.
If you say that because the Tathāgata [established] this seal, one is called a guardian of the precepts, then regarding this matter, you must be careful not to give rise to doubt!
The Tathāgata is without marks; therefore, he is called one who guards the precepts.
If it is said that the Tathāgata guards the precepts because of marks, do not give rise to doubt;
the Tathāgata is without the secondary signs of physical excellence; therefore, he is called one who guards the precepts.
If it is said that the Tathāgata is called one who upholds the precepts because of his primary marks and secondary signs, do not give rise to doubt;
the Tathāgata is not so named because of the causal conditions of supernatural powers, but is called one who guards the precepts.
The Tathāgata is not a secret treasury; therefore, it is called guarding the precepts.
The Tathāgata is not merely a supreme field of merit; therefore, it is called guarding the precepts.
The Tathāgata is not for the sake of the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, it is called guarding the precepts.
The Tathāgata maintains the precepts in order to sever all sentient beings from the oppression of the manifold sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death;
he maintains the precepts because he desires to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings;
and he maintains the precepts because he seeks to sever the bonds of birth and death for sentient beings.
It is called guarding the precepts because it causes sentient beings to single-mindedly direct themselves toward the path of unsurpassed bodhi;
it is called guarding the precepts because it enables all sentient beings to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
and it is called guarding the precepts because one desires to turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
It is called "guarding the precepts" because it causes all sentient beings to attain the name of the noble Saṅgha;
it is called "guarding the precepts" because it ensures that sentient beings do not sever the noble lineage of the Tathāgata;
it is called "guarding the precepts" because it ensures that sentient beings never sever the seeds of the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
It is called "guarding the precepts" because it causes all sentient beings to fully attain samādhi, dhyāna-concentration, wisdom, and liberation;
it is called "guarding the precepts" because it causes all sentient beings to fully attain pure precepts, complete and without deficiency;
and it is called "guarding the precepts" because the Tathāgata has no precepts.
It is called "guarding the precepts" because it severs all [conventional] precepts;
it is called "guarding the precepts" because the Tathāgata does not possess such precepts;
it is called "guarding the precepts" because he is not devoid of such precepts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Cloud Secret Treasury addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If it is said:”
Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata does not guard the precepts," what is its meaning? Furthermore,
if it is said that "a bodhisattva dwelling in this profound and advanced Samudra-velā-samādhi (Ocean Tide Samādhi) does not guard the precepts," what is its meaning?
"If the Tathāgata is not the Unsurpassed Seal, why is he called a 'Protector of the Precepts'?
What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! Since the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has dwelt in this samādhi, he has never from the beginning dwelt within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) while fully accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas.”
Why is this? Because this samādhi has already fully encompassed all Buddha-dharmas. Good son!
Just as a great heap of precious jewels contains blue lapis lazuli of pure color, such that those who see it do not give rise to doubt,
so too, from the moment a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained this samādhi, they clearly perceive the Buddha-nature without any uncertainty.
Why is this? Because it is seen with perfect clarity; if there were anyone who harbored doubt, such a thing would be impossible.
The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, they fully accomplish and perfect all the merits of the Buddhas.
“World-Honored One!”
“Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi attain the ultimate? “Good son,
you should not say:”
"Does such a bodhisattva attain ultimate [enlightenment]? Why is this?
If all sentient beings were to attain this samādhi and all achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, having reached ultimate completion, only then should one ask:
“Does this bodhisattva attain ultimate [realization]? “World-Honored One!
Such a samādhi is most rare; if sentient beings do not hear or receive it, they are truly to be pitied.”
"If anyone should hear this, you should know that such a person will obtain great benefit.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
If there are those who hear the name of this samādhi, you should know that such persons are the most eminent among men.

For example, they are like a noble prince of distinguished lineage: handsome, majestic, brave, and robust; his mind is free from stinginess, he maintains pure precepts, and he is beyond reproach. All people delight in seeing him, his kinsmen revere and cherish him, and as he governs the land, the people submit to him.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, it is likewise so: they fully accomplish all the merits of the Buddhas. "Good son!
It is like a caṇḍāla who can never become a king; if he were to become a king, such a thing would be impossible."
Why is this? Because they would be ridiculed by those of noble lineage and others.
If there are sentient beings who cannot receive, uphold, recite, or transcribe such a samādhi, yet wish to achieve all the subtle and wondrous merits of the Buddhas, this is likewise impossible.
Why is this? Because they will be ridiculed by all the bodhisattvas. Good son!
Observe now these bodhisattvas who dwell securely in this samādhi; they are able to know that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging.
If there are those who cannot abide in this samādhi, they will be unable to know that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and without change.
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of sentient beings, receive, uphold, read, and recite such a samādhi, they then attain the fulfillment of the dāna-pāramitā. Why is this?

In this way, when a bodhisattva sees someone seeking anything—be it their head, eyes, marrow, brain, limbs, hands, or feet; their kingdom, city, wife, children, slaves, servants, or attendants; or elephants, horses, and the seven treasures—they are able to provide such various gifts accordingly.
He is still willing to give away his own body, let alone external treasures;
he gives with joy and feels no regret after giving.
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whether it is attained or not, his mind is free from doubt or anxiety, and he never practices giving for the sake of a reward.
If one says that one practices giving for the sake of retribution, such a thing is impossible.
One does not practice giving out of greed;
rather, one practices bestowing gifts out of compassion.

For the sake of the Tathāgata’s permanence, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, and desiring to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā, they practice giving by proclaiming that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging.
"Furthermore, good son!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, he is able to know to some extent that all sentient beings possess buddha-nature, and that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi constantly contemplates thus:
"This body of mine is now empty and devoid of anything; I have already attained the matter of unsurpassed, great benefit."
I now give these limbs, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, brain, flesh, skin, blood, and sinews as alms to others, so that in the future I may attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, how does he practice such contemplation of the body? “Good son!

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not perceive this body as coming or going, sitting or reclining; it is like an empty bottle. Therefore, when the bodhisattva contemplates the body as empty and quiescent—its blood, flesh, marrow, and bones—it is called the "empty body."
"Bodhisattvas who dwell in this samādhi attain a body that is not of flesh, blood, bone, or marrow; they accomplish the Dharma-body and are not called 'food-bodies.
" [The Bodhisattva asked: "World-Honored One!"
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not called the "Food-body"; what is the meaning of this?
Since the Dharma-body has no form and cannot be seen, how does it bring about the transformation and guidance of sentient beings?
The Tathāgata has often said in various sūtras: "Just as a bird flying through the sky leaves no tracks, so too is the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata;
it neither comes nor goes, it neither transforms nor speaks, and it is indestructible."
The Mahāvaipulya Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Five;
The Mahāvaipulya Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
The Great Cloud Sūtra, First Division, The Chapter on Increasing Vigor, Part Three of Thirty-Seven.
The Buddha said: “Good son!
"Do not speak such words!
The body of the sentient beings transformed by the Tathāgata is what is called the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).
"World-Honored One! [he asked.]
What is the meaning of this, World-Honored One?
According to what the Buddha has taught, one who abides in this samādhi attains the Dharma-body; why, then, do you further say that it is the transformation body?
If the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata manifests as a body that consumes various foods for the sake of teaching and transforming beings, how can this body not be illusory?
As for the true Dharma-body, how could it again become a body that consumes various foods?
"If it were to constitute a body of food, that meaning would not be correct.
The Buddha said: "Stop, stop!
"Do not speak such words!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, if there is a manifested body, it is called an illusory body.
"World-Honored One!"
Why is this a perversion?
Because that which is not the body is called "body.
That which has no substance is termed an illusion.
“If it is an illusory body, how can it avoid deceiving sentient beings?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Do not hold such a view!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi has no abiding body.
Although he has no abiding body, he is like the king of medicinal trees, and like grass, wood, tiles, and pebbles.
My body is also like this.
Why? Because my body is without self, without what belongs to a self, without life, without speech, without mind, without reality, and without the aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
Just as a medicinal tree can eliminate all the suffering of illness for sentient beings, so too is my body;
it extinguishes the immeasurable suffering of illness for sentient beings. Why is this?
"Because the body is like an illusion.
Furthermore, son of good family!
It is like a medicinal tree, which never gives rise to the thought:"
"Take the leaves, do not take the branches.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva never gives rise to the thought:
"Take my hand, do not take my feet."
Why is this? It is because by the power of this samādhi, one is also able to eliminate and sever the maladies of greed, hatred, and delusion in all sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, there is no internal body, no external body, no internal-external body, and no body of birth and death; they attain the ambrosial body.
Because they possess the ambrosial body, they are able to sever the maladies of sentient beings—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion.
"Furthermore, noble son!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi manifests transformation bodies to sever all evils for birds, beasts, and those in the three evil realms, acting like a medicinal tree."
If anyone should say:
"Evil birds and beasts, upon encountering the body of a Bodhisattva, fall into the three evil realms," such a thing is impossible.
If it is said:
"One casts off this body and transmigrates to the realms of humans and devas to behold the Buddhas," such a thing is possible.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If it is said:
"If the fourfold assembly dwells in this samādhi, they will then be able to draw near to immeasurable Buddhas," this is indeed possible.
"Furthermore, good son!
If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās wish to practice this samādhi, they should first reflect:
'The Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and without change;'"
"The Buddha-dharma shall not perish, and there shall be none who enter final nirvana. He further thought:

"Whatever various necessities all sentient beings may require, I shall provide and bestow them; whether it be my feet, my hands, my head, or my eyes—for the sake of the True Dharma, I shall relinquish everything I possess."
One rejoices at the time of relinquishing, and having relinquished, one has no regrets.
Why is this? This body of mine is like a medicinal tree.
"If one can engage in such a single thought-moment of reflection, you should know that before long, one will attain this samādhi. Furthermore, good son!
It is like a fine horse, whose mane and tail are slender and long."
On the fifteenth day of the uposatha, in the midst of the great ocean, he cried out three times with a mournful voice:
"Who wishes to cross the sea!
Who wishes to cross the sea!"
"If there are people who mount its back, or grasp its mane, tail, neck, head, or legs, they shall all reach the further shore of the great ocean."

This *Mahāmegha Sūtra* is likewise; if there are those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, or transcribe it—even down to a single phrase, a single character, or two words—they shall all cross to the other shore of the three evil realms and attain eternal liberation.
"Furthermore, good son!

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās should hear the name of this samādhi, in every successive birth they will always become a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), Śakra, or Brahmā, never regressing, and will always be able to draw near to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the noble Saṅgha."
"Regarding the bodhicitta, one remains firm and unshakable, never abandoning the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
"World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in this samādhi, perceive all dharmas with perfect correctness?"
The Buddha said:

"Good son! If there are those who, having accomplished this samādhi, perceive the Tathāgata as impermanent, without bliss, without self, without purity, and as ultimate nirvāṇa, then what they see cannot be called truly correct."
"If one perceives the Tathāgata as eternal, blissful, self, and pure, and understands that he never ultimately enters parinirvāṇa, this is what is called seeing with true correctness.
"World-Honored One! [The assembly said.]
"As the Buddha has said:
'If one perceives the Tathāgata as permanent, blissful, self, and pure,' what is the meaning of this? "Good son!
“Permanence, bliss, self, and purity are precisely the true nature of the Tathāgata.
“World-Honored One!
If this is so, then all ordinary beings would also achieve such a true nature.”
Why is this? Ordinary people likewise calculate [the self] as permanent, blissful, self, and pure. "Good son!

You should not speak in such a manner now. What I say is that only a bodhisattva who possesses these samādhis is able to perceive the permanence, bliss, self, and purity; I am not speaking of the inverted permanence, bliss, self, and purity imagined by ordinary people.
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:

‘If one perceives all phenomena as impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity, this person then perceives the higher path and the lower path, attains the fruit of srotāpanna, and even attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;”
If one perceives all phenomena as permanent, blissful, self, and pure, then one cannot attain the fruit of srotāpanna, up to and including anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"How is it that the World-Honored One says:
'Once a bodhisattva has accomplished this samādhi, they shall see the permanent, the blissful, the self, and the pure'?
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
“True liberation is like empty space; such liberation is itself nirvāṇa.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata say:

“Nirvāṇa is eternal, blissful, self, and pure,” while also saying that all sentient beings are like empty space, the moon in water, dreams, illusions, plantain trees, clouds, and lightning—empty, devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics, unable to abide for even a moment, just like drawing on water, where as soon as one draws, it immediately merges back together?

To perceive and realize that there is no permanence, no pleasure, no self, and no purity—to see such characteristics is called true seeing. One who possesses true seeing attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and even proceeds to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"How is it that the Tathāgata says:
'A bodhisattva who accomplishes this samādhi shall then perceive permanence, bliss, self, and purity'?
As the Buddha previously stated:

"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, contemplate all phenomena as impermanent, without pleasure, without self, and without purity; they are devoid of life-span, a person, or a sentient being; they are empty and non-existent—this is called the true nature of all phenomena."
"Now you further say:
'I see all dharmas as permanent, blissful, self, and pure. What is the meaning of this? "Good son!
Stop, stop! Do not speak such words!
O son of good family!

If a bodhisattva has accomplished and perfected this samādhi, they no longer engage in conjunction with or non-conjunction with any dharmas; thus, they are named a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who guards the precepts and cultivates samādhi. They do not perceive the marks of annihilation or permanence in any dharmas. Because they do not perceive annihilation, they do not give rise to joy; because they do not perceive permanence, they do not give rise to sorrow. This is for the sake of knowing the seal of the Dharma (dharmamudrā), and not for the sake of guarding the precepts; furthermore, such a person cannot be said to be "cultivating samādhi."
