The Tathāgata does not cling to the observance of precepts or their violation; to permanence or impermanence; to awakening or non-awakening; to action or non-action; to purity or impurity; to emptiness or non-emptiness; to morality or non-morality; to knowledge or non-knowledge; to names or non-names; to grasping or non-grasping; to fear or non-fear; to dread or non-dread; to causes or non-causes; to cessation or non-cessation; to bodhi or non-bodhi; to liberation or non-liberation; or to nirvāṇa or non-nirvāṇa.
All dharmas are devoid of fear; for the sake of liberation, one upholds the prohibitions and precepts and cultivates samādhi.

All dharmas are without retrogression or extinction; having realized this, the Bodhisattva’s mind finds joy and cultivates this samādhi. For the sake of all sentient beings, he proclaims that the Buddha-Tathāgata is eternal and unchanging, and that the True Dharma does not perish; therefore, he guards the precepts and cultivates samādhi.
Furthermore, good son!

If there is anyone who wishes to attain such a samādhi, they should cultivate the perception of permanence, the perception of self, the perception of life, and the perception of a person. Having practiced these perceptions, one will then achieve and possess this samādhi; it is impossible that one would not attain it.
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity, yet at other times he speaks of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. What is the meaning of this?”

“Good son! Those on the mundane path erroneously perceive all phenomena as permanent, blissful, self, and pure; therefore, I teach that they are impermanent, non-self, without bliss, and without purity.”
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the supramundane Dharma, can it possibly possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity? “Good son!”
If there is a bodhisattva who, dwelling in this samādhi, wishes to speak of the self, he first speaks of five things. What are these five?
First, grain seeds; second, tree seeds; third, rich flavors; fourth, hidden treasures; and fifth, snake sloughs.
"Good son! For example, a grain seed is called impermanent during the stages of sprouting, stem formation, leafing, and flowering;
yet when it bears fruit and sentient beings enjoy its use, it is then called permanent."
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has not yet accomplished this samādhi, there is no permanence, no self, no bliss, and no purity;
if they have already accomplished it, then they are said to possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
If one has not yet been able to deliver all sentient beings, it is termed impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity;
if one is able to deliver them, it is then termed permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
If one cannot destroy all false views, they are termed impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity;
if one can destroy them, they are then termed permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Because one cannot eternally sever all afflictions, they are termed impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
if one can eternally sever them, these are then termed permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Good son! This is called a grain seed. Furthermore, good son!"
Just as with the mango tree, when it has not yet borne fruit, it is termed impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure;
but once the fruit is obtained and enjoyed by sentient beings, it is then termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has not yet attained this samādhi, it is termed impermanent, non-self, without bliss, and impure;
once they have attained it, it is then termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
Because they have not yet been able to deliver all sentient beings, they are termed impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
if they are able to deliver them, they may then be termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
If one cannot destroy all false views, they are termed impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
if one can destroy them, they are then termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
Because one cannot eternally sever all afflictions, they are termed impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
if one can eternally sever them, they may then be termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
"Good son! This is called the tree seed. Furthermore, good son!"

Just as when sesame seeds have not yet produced oil, they cannot eliminate the sickness and suffering of sentient beings and are thus termed impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity;
once the oil has been produced, it can remove all the sickness and suffering of sentient beings, and for this reason it is termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has not yet accomplished this samādhi, it is termed impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity;
once it has been accomplished, it is then termed permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Because they have not yet been able to deliver all sentient beings, they are termed impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure;
if they were able to deliver them, they could then be termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
That which cannot destroy all false views is called impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity;
that which can destroy them is called permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Because one cannot eternally sever all afflictions, they are termed impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
if one can eternally sever them, these are then termed permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Good son! This is called 'fattening flavor. Furthermore, good son!"
Suppose there were a treasure trove hidden beneath the earth; as long as it cannot benefit all sentient beings, it is termed impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure.
Once it has emerged from the earth and sentient beings enjoy its use, it becomes a source of great benefit; this is then termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet accomplished this samādhi, they are said to be without permanence, without bliss, without self, and without purity;
once it has been accomplished, they are then said to possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Because they have not yet been able to deliver all sentient beings, they are termed impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
if they are able to deliver them, they may then be termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
If one cannot destroy all false views, they are termed impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity;
if one can destroy them, these are then termed permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Because one cannot eternally sever all afflictions, they are termed impermanent, non-self, without bliss, and impure;
if one can eternally sever them, they are then termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
"Good son! This is called the 'Jewel Treasury. Furthermore, good son!"
It is like a snake shedding its skin: while it has not yet shed its skin, it is called impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
once it has shed its skin, it is then called permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has not yet accomplished this samādhi, it is termed impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity;
once they have accomplished it, it is then termed permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
When one has not yet been able to deliver all sentient beings, it is termed impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity;
if one can deliver them, then it may be termed permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
If one cannot destroy all false views, they are termed impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
if one can destroy them, they are then termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
Because they cannot permanently sever all afflictions, they are termed impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;

if they can permanently sever them, they are then termed permanent, blissful, self, and pure, and furthermore, they sever the fourfold doubts regarding permanence, bliss, self, and purity that sentient beings harbor toward the Buddha.
"Good son! This is called the slough of a snake. Good son!"

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, by means of these five matters, they expound the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity; they can speak of the self, the person, the life-span, sentient beings, and the individual; to be able to see in this way is called right view.
“World-Honored One!
These five matters spoken of by the Tathāgata are not so in meaning. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has constantly taught in various sūtras that all dharmas are impermanent.
As with the five matters mentioned above, the cause is impermanent and the fruit is also impermanent.
If a bodhisattva were to abide in this samādhi, then like those five matters, it too should be impermanent.
For this reason, O World-Honored One, among all dharmas, there is none that is not impermanent.
Where there is a cause, there must be an effect; where there is an effect, there must be a cause. It is the same for all sentient beings and all bodhisattvas.

Where there is birth, there must be death; where there is death, there must be birth. If this is so, then the permanent is impermanent and the impermanent is permanent. For this reason, all phenomena possess two natures: permanence and impermanence.
One should not categorically state that worldly phenomena are impermanent and supramundane phenomena are permanent.
“The Tathāgata speaks words of truth; how could he utter such false speech?
“Good son, why do you now entangle yourself like a silkworm in its cocoon?”
"Good son! If someone were to say:
'A person of handsome appearance is like the full moon;'"
"The fragrant elephant is beautiful and white, just like the Snowy Mountains.
In reality, the person is not the moon, nor is the elephant the Snowy Mountains; however, because there is a slight resemblance, it is cited as a metaphor.
Good son! The five things in the world are likewise; because they possess a small degree of permanence, they are used as metaphors.
Although the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are truly beyond metaphor, these are still employed as metaphors for their sake.
“World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata is eternal, for what reason do you further state in other sūtras that liberation is just like the extinguishing of a lamp?”
World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata is permanent, how can he undergo extinction?
If he undergoes extinction, how can you say he is permanent?
If the Tathāgata were to say, "It is both eternal and subject to extinction," would such a statement not be false?
Furthermore, as the Buddha has said:
"All phenomena are like the moon reflected in water."
“If all dharmas are permanent, why do you further say they are ‘like the moon in water’?
“Good son! I speak of conditioned phenomena as being like the moon in water; therefore, I say that some dharmas are permanent and other dharmas are impermanent.”

If there are sentient beings who have not yet attained liberation, have not yet severed afflictions, have not yet severed names and marks, have not yet severed the mark of a sentient being, have not attained the mark of dharmas, and have not yet attained the cultivation of such samādhi, this is called impermanence.

If there are sentient beings who have already attained liberation, have forever severed afflictions, names and marks, and the mark of a sentient being, have attained the mark of dharmas, and cultivate samādhi, this is called permanence.
"Therefore, I say that some dharmas are permanent and other dharmas are impermanent.
"World-Honored One, if that is so,
for what reason did the Tathāgata say:"
"Does the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa resemble the extinguishing of a lamp?
If it is like the extinguishing of a lamp, does this metaphor signify the extinction of the body, or the extinction of the fetters (*saṃyojana*)?
Just as the oil is not separate from the lamp, and the lamp is not separate from the oil."
“Sentient beings are also like this: the body is not separate from the fetters, and the fetters are not separate from the body;
how can you say they are extinguished? The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!”
"Good son! To see in this way is called right view. Good son!"
There are two kinds of bodies:
first, the body of afflictions; second, the dharma-body.
When the body of afflictions is extinguished, it is like the extinguishing of a lamp; for this reason, I say that "all other phenomena are impermanent."
The Dharma-body is without extinction, just like empty space; therefore, I say that "other dharmas are eternal.

To sever the vessel of afflictions is called liberation. If one were to claim that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a non-eternal body after attaining liberation, this would be the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

Conversely, if one were to claim that the habitual tendencies of afflictions are eternally indestructible within the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, this would be the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, certainly do not possess these two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Having already, over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, severed these two views, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are free from them.
If the Tathāgata possessed the mark of a sentient being, he would be impermanent;
however, the Tathāgata has already severed the mark of a sentient being throughout immeasurable kalpas. To say that the Tathāgata possesses the mark of a sentient being is impossible.

“Good son! It is like a great king who goes out and about on inspection: when he is outside, he is not seen within; yet although he is not seen within, one cannot say he does not exist. It is the same with what is outside.”
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, although he has already severed impermanence, for the sake of sentient beings, he assumes an impermanent body.
If one were to say,
"The body of the Tathāgata is impermanent," such a thing is impossible.

For this reason, I speak of permanence and impermanence; I speak of self and non-self; I speak of sentient beings and non-sentient beings; I speak of persons and non-persons; I speak of life and non-life; I speak of individuals and non-individuals.
The Tathāgata has always taught:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
He never says they are permanent; were he to say they are permanent, it would be impossible.
"Furthermore, good son!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, he attains the severance of views of the world, views of the self as a life-principle, and views of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
he is free from craving and attachment, and has neither grasping nor seeking."
It is eternally unchanging, perfectly accomplished and abiding, and has attained fearlessness;
it is free from arrogance and cannot be defiled by impurities.
For this reason, I speak of "Eternity, Bliss, Self, and Purity."

"Good son! I speak of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, which are not understood by all worldly people; yet although worldly people do not understand them, one must never say that the wise are likewise [ununderstood]."
Although people of the world perceive the Tathāgata as impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity, one cannot say that those possessed of wisdom share such a view.
Those of meager merit, dull faculties, and those who follow false paths will say:
"The Tathāgata is impermanent; he has entered eternal extinction and nirvāṇa.
If one says, "The Tathāgata has entered eternal parinirvāṇa," you should know that such a person shall not escape the three evil realms.
“Good son! It is like a deep pool whose water is turbid; though there is a precious jewel within it, people do not see it.
Someone then cries out:”
"There is a great precious jewel in this turbid water!
Having heard this, the multitude vied with one another to search for it; some obtained shards, stones, gravel, grass, or wood, yet none were able to find the true treasure.
Because they could not find it, they declared it to be false and illusory.

Furthermore, there was another person who was skilled in expedient means; he placed a priceless jewel into turbid water, and the water immediately became clear, whereby all the people were able to see the true treasure.
"Good son! Because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not understand the power of such samādhi, they say:
'The Tathāgata is impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity; he is empty and non-existent.'"
Failing to realize that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging, they continue to revolve in birth and death.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, he skillfully understands all the secret words of the Tathāgata; for this reason, this priceless jewel is used as a metaphor for the samādhi.
"Good son! Whether a man or a woman, those who wish to see the Tathāgata as eternally constant and unchanging should practice this samādhi.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they see the Tathāgata as eternally constant and unchanging; liberation is likewise so."

“Good son! Just as the shade of a tree provides rest for those traveling on the road, so too it is with the bodhisattvas who abide in this samādhi; they act as a protective shade for all sentient beings.”
“Good son! If there is anyone who says, ‘The Tathāgata is impermanent and has entered eternal parinirvāṇa,’ such a person is a disciple of Māra;
if it is not so, they are truly my disciple.”
If one says, "The Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa," you should know that such a person defiles my Dharma; if there are those who believe and accept such words, they are truly to be pitied.

When these words were spoken, a great radiance issued forth from the right side of the assembly. This light was golden in color and illuminated the trichiliocosm, completely eclipsing the brilliance of the sun, the moon, and even Brahmā; yet it could not obscure the radiance of the Buddha, while all other lights became dark and invisible.
The great and small Mount Sumerus, the grasses, trees, and forests, and the dark and gloomy places between the two lands—there was no spot that was not brilliantly illuminated.
When the sentient beings in the hells encountered this light, their agonizing pains were stilled, and their bodies attained peace and happiness.

At that time, before the entire great assembly, there immediately emerged sixty trillion lotus flowers. These flowers were exquisite, endowed with perfect color and fragrance; each had a thousand full-blown petals and was composed of the four precious substances.
Each individual lotus emits a subtle and wondrous fragrance that pervades the trichiliocosm.

All beings therein—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, Māra, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all other sentient beings—having smelled this fragrance, all come to love the Dharma, find joy in the Mahāyāna, delight in hearing the Dharma, and sever all afflictions. Such are the merits and subtle fragrances accomplished by these flowers.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmeghagambhīrakośa, being within the great assembly, beheld this miraculous manifestation. He immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverent salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of appearance is this?
By whose power of merit does it arise?
Within this great assembly, there are these wondrous flowers that emit immeasurable fragrance?
Thereupon, the goddess Viśuddhaprabhā addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāmeghagambhīrakośa, saying:
"O son of good family!
All phenomena are entirely without marks; why do you ask:?"
"What kind of appearance is this?
All phenomena are like dreams; why do you ask such a question in a state of delusion, as if possessed by madness?
Mahāmeghagambhīragarbha replied:
“Excellent, excellent, O goddess!
It is not that I do not see all phenomena as being like a dream; however, I ask this for the purpose of severing attachment to signs.”
The goddess said, "Venerable sir!
Why do you perceive signs and give rise to this question?"
“O Goddess! For this reason, I previously said:
‘It is for the sake of sentient beings, wishing to bring them across and liberate them, that I ask.’”
“Venerable Sir! If one does not sever one’s own view of self and one’s own doubt, how can one deliver sentient beings?
If one does not sever one’s own view of self and one’s own doubt, it is impossible to eliminate the views and doubts of sentient beings.”
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”
It is indeed as the goddess has proclaimed:
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, he perceives only the signless.
Son of good family!
Whether a man or a woman, those who wish to see the signless (*animitta*) should practice this samādhi with diligent effort.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they are able to manifest various bodies throughout the trichiliocosm.
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva, abiding in this samādhi, manifest various bodies throughout the trichiliocosm? “Good son!”

Suppose there were a master illusionist or an illusionist’s disciple who, in the midst of a great assembly, could produce various forms—whether male or female, large or small, living or dead, going or coming, houses or forests, elephants or horses—and could cause them to be severed or broken, split or destroyed, and then restored or made to vanish.
When the great assembly saw this, they felt no surprise or wonder.
Why was this? Because they understood it to be an illusion.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling in this samādhi and cultivating the right path, they manifest various bodies within this trichiliocosm for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
When bodhisattvas dwelling in this samādhi see these emanations, they do not give rise to alarm or wonder; they have no doubt, but accord with the meaning without any opposition.
Why is this? It is because one knows with certainty that it is due to the power of samādhi. "Furthermore, good son!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this samādhi, they are able to manifest their bodies in various places throughout the trichiliocosm, in accordance with the diverse modes of conduct of all sentient beings.
Alternatively, he may manifest within a mother’s womb in Jambudvīpa; all sentient beings truly see the Bodhisattva dwelling in the womb, yet that Bodhisattva does not actually reside in the womb.

Alternatively, he may manifest his entry into the womb in Jambudvīpa, and sentient beings likewise see the Bodhisattva emerging from the womb, yet this Bodhisattva does not actually emerge from the womb.

Or, he may manifest the first shaving of his hair in Jambudvīpa and the fashioning of the *cūḍā* topknot, such that all sentient beings perceive it as such; yet, in reality, the Bodhisattva possesses no such characteristic.

Or, in Jambudvīpa, he may manifest going to schools to practice various arts, calligraphy, and mathematics; all sentient beings see the Bodhisattva beginning his initial studies, yet this Bodhisattva has already completed all such training throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past.

Or, in Jambudvīpa, he may manifest as a human, a lion, or a white goose; all sentient beings see the Bodhisattva manifesting as a human, a lion, or a white goose, yet the Bodhisattva possesses none of these characteristics whatsoever.

In Jambudvīpa, it may appear that there are wives and children, and that one enjoys the pleasures of the five desires; all sentient beings perceive these signs. Yet this bodhisattva has long since distanced himself from such things in past kalpas, finding delight only in the joy of the Dharma.

Or, if it appears that the Bodhisattva in Jambudvīpa is voiding excrement or urinating, all sentient beings likewise perceive this phenomenon; yet, since this Bodhisattva has attained the true Dharma-body and not a body sustained by mixed food, how could there be excrement or urine?

Chewing on a tooth-stick, putting on clothes, washing the hands, stepping into leather sandals, holding a parasol, wearing necklaces upon the body, eating and drinking, hunger and thirst, birth, old age, sickness, and death.
By practicing the perfection of giving, one becomes a wheel-turning monarch, possessing male and female slaves, servants, sons and daughters, both great and small;
or one may become a human or a deva, practicing the asceticism of a dhūta.
He manifests as a bhikṣu to bring benefit and welfare to sentient beings.
He manifests the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat;
yet he also disrupts the Saṃgha, listens to and preaches the Dharma, eats poisoned rice, violates the four grave prohibitions, and commits the five heinous crimes.

He manifests the forms of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, leaves the household life to study the Way, turns the wheel of the True Dharma beneath the Bodhi tree, displays great supernormal powers, and enters into nirvāṇa.
"Or they may become Śakra, Brahmā, or the Māra Pāpīyān, transmigrating through the various realms of existence like the wheel of a chariot;
it is just so, O son of good family."

Although Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas perform these various worldly practices in accordance with the world for the sake of liberating beings, they never give rise to the notion of "sentient beings," but constantly cultivate the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa).
Why is this? It is because of the power of this samādhi.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no place of attachment; he does not cling to the Śrāvakas, nor does he cling to the Pratyekabuddhas. Out of a desire to have compassion for all the world and to deliver sentient beings, he manifests his body in every place, according to their inclinations.
Therefore, the bodhisattva cultivates the signless and perceives the signless.
If a person can perceive such signlessness, this is called right view.
The goddess Viśuddhaprabhā also cultivates the signless.
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, abide in this samādhi; therefore, they are inconceivable.
"World-Honored One!
This goddess Pure Light has fully accomplished and perfected profound wisdom."
"If the realm of signlessness is inconceivable, then the one who cultivates it is likewise inconceivable.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance, and from his face issued forth immeasurable light.

That light was of five colors, illuminating immeasurable and boundless worlds above as far as the Brahma realm; it pervaded everything everywhere, circled his body three times, and returned to enter through his mouth.

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways, becoming adorned and pure like Uttarakuru; the trichiliocosm was likewise so transformed, and by the Buddha’s spiritual power, all sentient beings were able to behold it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmeghaghanagarbha rose again from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition, O son of good family, has this radiance been emitted?
The Buddha said:
"Son of good family!"
Regarding that which you have just doubted, I now wish to answer; therefore, I have emitted this auspicious sign of radiant light. Noble son!
To the west of here, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.

In that land there is a Buddha named Amitāyus, who currently dwells in the world, constantly preaching and proclaiming the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. He addresses a bodhisattva, saying:
"O son of good family!..."

In this Sahā world, Śākyamuni Buddha is preaching the *Mahāmegha Sūtra* for the sake of sentient beings with little merit and dull faculties; you should go there and listen to it with a sincere heart.
"This is because those bodhisattvas, wishing to come here, have first manifested these auspicious omens. Good son!
Observe the bodies of the bodhisattvas in that land; they are five thousand six hundred yojanas in height."
“World-Honored One!
What is the name of that bodhisattva who has come?
For what reason, moreover, has he come to this land?”
"Could it not be that he has come for the sake of delivering sentient beings?
I pray only that the Tathāgata will analyze and explain this for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Good son! [The Buddha replied.]
The bodhisattvas from that land have come because they wish to hear the specific account of the prediction of Vimalaprabhā, and because they desire to make offerings to this samādhi. Good son!
"This bodhisattva is named Anantaprabha; he has mastered skillful means and is well able to instruct others.
"World-Honored One!
We pray that the Tathāgata will tell us: at the place of which Buddha did this goddess first resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
"When shall I ever attain the transformation of this female body? "Good son!
You should not now ask about the transformation of the female body."

As for this heavenly maiden, she has constantly manifested in a female body for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas; you should know that this is a body of skillful means and not an actual female body.
How could one say: "When shall I transform this female body?
O son of good family!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, their body is sovereign, enabling them to employ various skillful means as appropriate.
Although they may assume the form of a woman, their mind is free from greedy attachment, and they remain untainted by the fetters of desire.
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that the Tathāgata will, for the sake of all sentient beings, explain the future affairs of this heavenly maiden. “Good son!”
Listen attentively now!
I shall explain it to you.
By means of skillful expedients, seven hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a small kingdom in South India named Avijñapti.
In that country there is a river named Black Darkness; on its southern bank there is a city named Ripe Grain, and in that city there is a king named Equal Vehicle.
The king’s consort gave birth to a daughter named Vardhanī; she was of upright and majestic form, beloved and respected by all, and she maintained the prohibitive precepts with diligent perseverance.

Because this daughter was born, the king’s realm experienced abundant harvests of grain and immeasurable happiness; the population flourished, free from decline, disease, suffering, anxiety, fear, or calamity, and all auspicious matters were fully accomplished.
The neighboring kings all came to submit and seek his protection.
Yet, as with all conditioned phenomena, there is impermanence and succession; that king could not escape it and suddenly passed away.
"At that time, the ministers immediately presented this girl to succeed to the royal lineage.
Once she had ascended the throne, her majesty subdued all under heaven; every land within Jambudvīpa came to serve her, and none dared to resist or disobey."

The Queen, possessing sovereign power, subdued all false views; desiring to make offerings to the Buddha’s relics, she erected stupas made of the seven precious gems throughout Jambudvīpa, and carried various colored silks, exquisite banners and canopies, and wonderful sandalwood incense to perform offerings everywhere.
Seeing those who protect the Dharma and uphold the pure precepts, he makes offerings to and reveres them;
seeing those who break the precepts and destroy the true Dharma, he rebukes and disgraces them, causing them to be extinguished without remainder.

Fully cultivating the ten pāramitās, upholding the five precepts, rescuing the poor and destitute, and instructing all immeasurable sentient beings by preaching the *Mahāmegha Sūtra* to harmonize their minds.
If one hears this Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtra, one shall reverently make offerings to it, honoring and praising it.
For twenty full years, one shall uphold, recite, copy, and explain this *Mahāmegha Sūtra*. Only then, upon the exhaustion of one's lifespan, shall one be able to transform this female body.
"For the sake of sentient beings, he manifests great supernormal powers; desiring to make offerings to Amitāyus Buddha, he has been born in that realm.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]
“Will this queen, in the future, attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? “Good son, this queen,

in a future age after immeasurable kalpas have passed, shall become a Buddha named Viśuddha-tattva-vardhana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.”

At that time, this Sahā world was renamed Purely Washed; there was a city named Pure and Sublime Fragrance, which was adorned entirely with the seven treasures, most excellent and unsurpassed, like the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
That city contains ninety trillion people; the land is level and even, free from thorns, sand, grit, and stones. The people of that land do not give rise to false views and cherish the Mahāyāna.

There were no names of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; all were exclusively bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who cultivated the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, achieved patience, and possessed immeasurable lifespans.
“Good son! If there are sentient beings who hear the name of that Buddha-Tathāgata, they shall not fall into the three evil realms but will instead be reborn among humans and devas.
Having spoken this sutra, immeasurable sentient beings attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
